title: Devin's 2025 Performance Review: Learnings from 18 Months of Agents at Work
description: Cognition writes an annual performance review for its AI software engineer — the agent-as-employee metaphor done with real data from deployments at Goldman Sachs and Santander: 67% PR merge rate (up from 34%), 20x efficiency on vulnerability fixes, strong on clearly-scoped junior tasks, weak on ambiguous requirements and mid-task scope changes. A template for how organizations should evaluate agent 'staff' by role fit rather than raw capability.
why: Treating an agent as an employee with an annual review is the agent-as-staff framing taken further than most teams go.

title: Factory Is GA: Droids for the Entire SDLC
description: Factory's general-availability launch of purpose-built 'droids' — role-scoped agents covering distinct SDLC functions: end-to-end coding, PR review, on-call incident resolution, deep codebase research, ticket management, and product specs. An early commercial commitment to explicit role boundaries (the reviewer never silently patches its own complaints) rather than one generalist agent.
why: Role-scoped agents covering distinct parts of the lifecycle, a commercial bet on specialization over generality.

title: A One-Person AI-Agent Company: Every Role Is a Folder
description: Widely-shared concrete artifact of an org graph in the wild: a company run by 6 agents and 20 cron jobs where 'every role is a folder, every job description is a md file' — roles as version-controlled configuration, schedules replacing standups. Saboo later co-articulated the org-graph/work-graph distinction in the July 2026 graph-engineering discourse, making this the practice that preceded the theory.
why: A concrete org graph in the wild, with roles as folders and schedules as the coordination mechanism.

title: The Code Agent Orchestra: What Makes Multi-Agent Coding Work
description: Osmani (Google Chrome engineering lead) on moving from a single synchronous 'conductor' agent to an asynchronous orchestra: subagents with clear ownership boundaries, agent teams with shared task lists and peer messaging, and hierarchical delegation where feature leads spawn their own specialists. Argues verification, not generation, is the bottleneck, and that plan-approval gates catch architectural flaws early. Published March 26, 2026.
why: Moving from one synchronous conductor to parallel specialists, described by someone who ran both.

title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real-World Tasks
authors: Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, Graham Neubig, et al.
description: A fully simulated software company — self-hosted GitLab, Plane, ownCloud, RocketChat, and 16 LLM-simulated colleagues with personas — testing agents on 175 long-horizon professional tasks across engineering, PM, HR, finance, and admin. Best agents complete ~30% autonomously, with social/coordination tasks (HR ~18%) failing far more than coding (~42%): the sobering baseline for anyone claiming agents can staff an organization.
why: A simulated company with real tooling is the closest available test of whether an agent org can hold a job.

title: Measuring and Mitigating Identity Bias in Multi-Agent Debate via Anonymization
description: Shows debate agents weight WHO said something over WHAT was said — with conformity (sycophancy) generally exceeding obstinacy — causing premature consensus that reinforces wrong answers, and demonstrates response anonymization as a concrete fix. Direct design guidance for council nodes: strip author identity from edges before deliberation.
why: Debate agents weighting who spoke over what was said is a direct threat to any verification built on discussion.

title: Too Polite to Disagree: Understanding Sycophancy Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems
description: Documents how sycophancy propagates through agent organizations: instead of correcting each other, agents amplify each other's agreement patterns into collective conformity that entrenches errors. A 2026 empirical warning that stacking agreeable agents in a council produces confident consensus, not error correction — and why deliberation topologies need dissent mechanisms.
why: Documents sycophancy propagating through an organization, which is why agreement between nodes is weak evidence.

title: llm-council: A Council of LLMs with a Chairman
description: Karpathy's minimal working council: a query fans out to a fixed panel of frontier models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4 via OpenRouter), members review and rank each other's anonymized answers to prevent favoritism, and a Chairman synthesizes the final response. A weekend hack that became the reference implementation of committee-of-rivals topology with a built-in anti-bias gate.
why: A minimal working council with a chairman, useful as the smallest honest implementation of panel verification.

title: MegaAgent: Autonomous Large-Scale LLM Agent Systems Without Predefined SOPs
description: Where MetaGPT hand-writes the org chart, MegaAgent generates it: agents recursively spawn subordinate groups sized to task complexity, with hierarchical coordination, parallel execution, and system-level monitoring but no predefined SOPs. Scaled to 590 agents in a national-policy simulation and built a working Gobang game in ~800 seconds — an early concrete instance of the org graph rewriting itself on evidence.
why: Generating the org chart rather than writing it is the frontier claim, and this is a concrete attempt at it.

title: Devin Can Now Manage Devins (MultiDevin)
description: Announcement of managed Devin fleets: one manager Devin scopes work, delegates to up to 10 worker Devins in isolated VMs, monitors progress, resolves conflicts, and merges successful output into a single branch or PR. The recommended workload profile — repetitive, isolated, objectively verifiable subtasks like migrations and lint sweeps — is a crisp statement of when flat manager-worker orgs pay off.
why: Managed fleets with a manager delegating to workers, shipped commercially rather than proposed.

title: Reverse Conway's Law and Agents
description: Debois (co-originator of DevOps) inverts Conway for the agent era: instead of asking how org structure shapes agent systems, he asks how embedding capable agents reshapes the human organization itself — with an accompanying AI Engineer conference talk. Short, but the sharpest statement of the bidirectional Conway question for agent orgs.
why: Inverting a well-known law for the agent era reframes org design as a choice rather than an inheritance.

title: The Coasean Singularity? Demand, Supply, and Market Design with AI Agents
authors: NBER (The Economics of Transformative AI volume)
description: NBER chapter examining what happens to markets and organizational boundaries as agents drive transaction costs toward zero — instant preference elicitation, automated contracting — while creating new costs around trust and verification. The rigorous economics counterpart to practitioner essays on whether to organize agents as a 'firm' (org graph) or a market.
why: Asks what happens to organizational boundaries when transaction costs collapse, which is the economics behind agent staffing.

title: From Coase to AI Agents: Why the Economics of the Firm Still Matters in the Age of Automation
description: Applies Coase's 1937 transaction-cost theory of the firm to agents: if AI slashes the costs of search, negotiation, and monitoring, the efficient boundary between doing work inside an agent organization versus buying it from outside shifts — and may shrink firms. The clearest bridge from classical org economics to the question of where an agent org's edges should stop.
why: Applies transaction-cost theory to agents, giving a principled answer to which work belongs inside one organization.

title: The Future of Team Topologies: When AI Agents Dominate
description: The Team Topologies organization asks how its own framework survives teams that are 50-90% agents: Dunbar's-number limits on team size dissolve, communication has no social cost, and Conway's law must be re-read when the 'communicators' are programmable. First-party org-theory engagement with agent teams from the people who wrote the standard book on human team design.
why: A widely used team-design framework confronting mostly-agent teams, useful for anyone mapping human structures onto graphs.

title: CrewAI Agents: Role, Goal, Backstory
description: Documentation for the most popular role-first framework: every agent is declared with a required role (function and expertise), goal (decision-making objective), and backstory (context and personality), composed into crews with sequential or hierarchical processes. The de facto standard for expressing an org graph's roles as declarative config, used in production well before the graph-engineering label existed.
why: The role, goal, and backstory contract shows what a framework considers the minimum specification of a node.

title: Claude Code: Create Custom Subagents
description: Official docs for defining named agent roles as configuration: each subagent gets its own system prompt, context window, tool allowlist, permission mode, and model choice, and the main agent delegates when a task matches the role's description. The most widely used mechanism in 2026 for encoding an org graph's 'who' — reusable role definitions that persist across projects.
why: Defining roles as configuration with their own prompts and tools is role design made version-controllable.

title: Examining Identity Drift in Conversations of LLM Agents
description: Empirical study of role drift across nine LLMs: agent interaction styles and identities shift over multi-turn conversations, larger models drift MORE, and assigning a persona does not reliably anchor identity. The core evidence base for why stable org-graph roles need active maintenance (persona re-injection, memory refresh) rather than a one-time system prompt.
why: Identity drift over long interactions is why a role needs enforcement, not just a good initial description.

title: Subagents — Agentic Engineering Patterns
description: Chapter of Willison's 'Agentic Engineering Patterns' guide on dispatching fresh specialist instances — code reviewers, debuggers, explorers — so the parent agent's token budget and context stay clean. A concise, vendor-neutral treatment of why specialist roles with isolated context beat one generalist loop, with parallel-subagent performance notes.
why: Dispatching fresh specialists with clean context is the most reusable pattern for keeping node context clean.

title: The Fable 5 Orchestrator Playbook: One Smart Model Managing Cheap Workers
description: Worked cost math for staffing org-graph nodes by model tier: frontier model for planning/dispatch/synthesis where errors compound, Sonnet-class for implementation, Haiku-class for read-only scouting. A 12-worker codebase audit runs $3.70 with cheap workers vs $14.50 all-frontier (74% savings), with the key asymmetry stated plainly — downgrading workers saves far more than downgrading the orchestrator. Includes honest counter-cases (shallow fan-outs, latency-sensitive flows).
why: Worked cost arithmetic for mixed-tier staffing, which turns a staffing intuition into a number you can check.

title: Orchestrator and Subagent Multi-Agent Patterns
description: Microsoft's guidance on hierarchical orgs where an orchestrator delegates to child agents or externally-owned 'connected agents' maintained by other teams — an explicit treatment of independent ownership and reuse as org-design criteria. Unusually honest about when NOT to use the pattern: compliance-grade consistency needs, well-defined step sequences, and latency-sensitive flows. Updated February 2026.
why: Vendor guidance on hierarchical delegation, useful as a baseline for what a supervisor node is expected to do.

title: langgraph-supervisor: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems
description: LangChain's library for building supervisor orgs on LangGraph: a central supervisor routes tasks to specialist worker agents and multi-level hierarchies are built by making supervisors manage supervisors. Useful both as working code and as a reference implementation of the supervisor pattern; LangChain now recommends the tool-calling variant for finer context control, which the repo documents.
why: A ready supervisor implementation, which lowers the cost of trying hierarchy before committing to it.

title: AI Agent Memory Architectures for Multi-Agent Systems: Shared, Isolated, Hierarchical
description: Systematic comparison of the three memory topologies — fully shared (noise and permission leakage), fully isolated (coordination overhead), hierarchical global/team/private (the industry convergence point) — with framework-by-framework analysis of CrewAI, LangGraph, and AutoGen and a review of conflict-resolution strategies. Cites the MAST finding that most multi-agent failures are coordination, not capability.
why: Compares shared, isolated, and hybrid memory directly, which is the decision every multi-agent design must make explicitly.

title: The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System: Integrating Knowledge to Resolve Uncertainty
authors: Lee Erman, Frederick Hayes-Roth, Victor Lesser, Raj Reddy
description: The original blackboard system (CMU, 1971-76): independent knowledge sources cooperate solely by reading and writing a shared hierarchical blackboard, with opportunistic scheduling deciding who acts next. Every modern shared-scratchpad multi-agent design descends from this paper; free PDF at mas.cs.umass.edu/Documents/Erman_Hearsay80.pdf.
why: The original shared-state architecture, where cooperation happens entirely through reads and writes to a common structure.

title: Exploring Advanced LLM Multi-Agent Systems Based on Blackboard Architecture
description: First implementation of a full blackboard architecture for LLM agents: all roles share one public blackboard, a control unit selects which agent acts based on blackboard content, and rounds repeat until consensus. Matches state-of-the-art master-slave systems on reasoning and math benchmarks while spending fewer tokens — evidence that shared state can beat message passing on cost.
why: A full shared-state architecture for language agents, testing whether the classical idea survives modern nodes.

title: LLM-based Multi-Agent Blackboard System for Information Discovery in Data Science
description: Replaces the master-slave orchestration paradigm with a blackboard: a central agent posts requests to a shared board and subordinate agents volunteer answers, so the orchestrator never needs to know which agent holds what. 13-57% relative improvement in end-to-end task success over direct-communication baselines on data-discovery tasks.
why: Replacing central orchestration with a shared board changes who decides what happens next, which is a topology claim.

title: SagaLLM: Context Management, Validation, and Transaction Guarantees for Multi-Agent LLM Planning
description: Imports the Saga transaction pattern from distributed databases into agent graphs: persistent cross-agent memory, independent validation agents, checkpointing, and compensating actions so a partially-failed multi-agent plan rolls back consistently instead of leaving corrupted shared state. The most direct treatment of the two-agents-one-resource consistency problem in the literature.
why: Brings transaction guarantees to agent state, addressing the partial-write problem that breaks shared memory in practice.

title: Context Engineering for Agents (LangChain)
description: The write/select/compress/isolate taxonomy that became the standard vocabulary for agent state management: write context out to scratchpads and memories, select it back in, compress via summarization, and isolate by splitting across sub-agents or sandboxed environments. Maps each strategy to concrete LangGraph mechanisms.
why: The write, select, compress, and isolate vocabulary that made context management something teams can discuss precisely.

title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)
description: Treats the context window as a finite resource with diminishing returns and lays out the three long-horizon state strategies — compaction, structured note-taking (agentic memory persisted outside the window), and sub-agent architectures where detailed search context stays isolated in workers while the lead synthesizes condensed summaries. The token-economics framing for shared-vs-isolated state decisions.
why: Treats the context window as a budgeted resource, which is the discipline that keeps long-running nodes coherent.

title: How and when to build multi-agent systems (LangChain)
description: Reconciles the Cognition and Anthropic positions: read-heavy tasks (research) tolerate isolated parallel contexts, while write-heavy tasks (code) demand shared context because conflicting writes are expensive to merge. A practical decision rule for how much state to share across each edge of a work graph.
why: Reconciles the two dominant positions on multi-agent design by separating read-heavy from write-heavy work.

title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: Lessons from Building Manus
description: Argues the filesystem is 'the ultimate context': unlimited, persistent, directly operable by the agent, letting Manus keep the token window small by paging observations out to files and restoring them on demand. The founding statement of filesystem-as-agent-memory, plus KV-cache economics and recitation (todo.md) as attention management.
why: Argues the filesystem is the durable context layer, a practical answer to context limits that agents can operate directly.

title: Claude Code Agent Teams: Shared Task List, Mailboxes, and File Ownership
description: The shared-state substrate of a shipping agent org: a shared task list with dependency tracking and file-locked task claiming to prevent races, per-agent JSON mailboxes under ~/.claude/teams/, and the explicit guidance that teammates must own disjoint file sets because two agents editing one file leads to overwrites. Experimental (flag-gated) as of v2.1.x, July 2026.
why: A shipping implementation of shared task state with ownership rules, which is the concrete form of coordination infrastructure.

title: Claude Code: Run Parallel Sessions with Git Worktrees
description: Worktree-per-agent as a state strategy made first-class: claude --worktree gives each session an isolated working directory and branch under .claude/worktrees/, and subagents can declare isolation: worktree in frontmatter so parallel edits physically cannot collide — merging moves to git, where conflict resolution is a solved problem.
why: Isolation per agent as a first-class feature is what makes parallel writers safe without a merge protocol.

title: CrewAI Memory: Unified Scoped Memory for Agent Crews
description: CrewAI's 2026 rework replaced separate short-term/long-term/entity stores with one API over hierarchical scope trees (/agent/researcher, /project/alpha): all agents in a crew share crew memory unless given their own, with composite recency-relevance-importance scoring and non-blocking background writes with read barriers. A clean example of hierarchical (global/team/private) memory scoping.
why: One scoped memory API across a team, showing how a framework resolves whose memory is whose.

title: LangGraph Memory: Store, Namespaces, and Cross-Thread Sharing
description: The other half of LangGraph state: short-term thread-scoped memory via checkpoints vs long-term memory in a Store with hierarchical namespaces, recallable from any thread and any node. Covers semantic/episodic/procedural memory types and profile-vs-collection write patterns — the concrete API for shared memory across an agent organization.
why: Separates run-scoped from cross-run memory explicitly, which is the distinction most memory bugs come from.

title: State of AI Agent Memory 2026 (Mem0)
description: Vendor-authored but data-heavy annual snapshot of the memory-layer landscape: benchmark results across memory systems, the convergence on graph-plus-vector hybrids, and MCP emerging as the standard interface for sharing one memory layer across heterogeneous agents. Read alongside independent comparisons; useful for July-2026 currency.
why: A data-heavy snapshot of the memory-layer landscape, useful for calibration despite being vendor-authored.

title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
authors: Wujiang Xu, Zujie Liang, Kai Mei, Hang Gao, Juntao Tan, Yongfeng Zhang
description: Zettelkasten-style memory: each stored note gets generated attributes and is dynamically linked to related notes, and new memories can trigger evolution (rewriting) of old ones, so the memory network restructures itself instead of only appending. Evaluated across six foundation models; code on GitHub (agiresearch/A-mem).
why: Dynamically linked notes give a memory that reorganizes as it grows rather than accumulating flat records.

title: How to Design Multi-Agent Memory Systems for Production (Mem0)
description: The multi-scope pattern for agent-org memory: every write tagged with user_id / agent_id / run_id / app_id, composed at retrieval time, so private, shared, and session-scoped facts coexist in one store. Framework-agnostic — the same memory layer serves agents built in LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/AG2, and Strands.
why: Scoping every write by user, agent, and run is the practical pattern that keeps shared memory from becoming noise.

title: Letta: Multi-Agent Shared Memory Blocks
description: Attach one memory block to many agents and every writer's update is instantly visible to all readers — coordination through shared in-context state rather than messaging. Notably honest about concurrency: memory_insert is append-only and safe under simultaneous writers, while rethink-style rewrites can clobber each other.
why: Memory blocks attached to many agents make shared state explicit and immediately visible to all readers.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
authors: Prateek Chhikara, Dev Khant, Saket Aryan, Taranjeet Singh, Deshraj Yadav
description: The extract-consolidate-retrieve memory pipeline behind the most-adopted agent memory layer, plus a graph-based variant (Mem0g) for relational facts. On LOCOMO: 26% relative improvement over the OpenAI memory baseline with 91% lower p95 latency and >90% token savings versus full-context replay.
why: The extract, consolidate, and retrieve pipeline behind a widely adopted memory layer, with published benchmarks.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, et al. (UC Berkeley)
description: The paper that started OS-inspired agent memory: virtual context management pages data between the fixed context window (main memory) and external storage, with the agent editing its own memory via tools. Direct ancestor of Letta and of the memory-block abstraction now used for multi-agent shared state.
why: The paper that started operating-system framing for agent memory, and the ancestor of most current designs.

title: Memory Blocks: The Key to Agentic Context Management
description: The design rationale behind memory blocks: structured, labeled, size-limited segments of the context window that agents edit themselves and that can be shared, versioned, and templated across an organization of agents. Explains why block-level structure beats one undifferentiated scratchpad.
why: Explains why structured, size-limited memory segments beat free-form context accumulation for long-lived roles.

title: MemOS: A Memory OS for AI Systems
description: Treats memory as a schedulable system resource: the MemCube unit unifies plaintext, activation (KV-cache), and parameter-level memories with metadata, enabling composition, migration, and fusion between forms. The most complete 'operating system' blueprint for memory governance across fleets of agents; open-source implementation at github.com/MemTensor/MemOS.
why: Treating memory as a schedulable resource is the most ambitious current attempt to systematize agent state.

title: From Human Memory to AI Memory: A Survey on Memory Mechanisms in the Era of LLMs
authors: Yaxiong Wu, Sheng Liang, et al. (Huawei Noah's Ark Lab)
description: The broadest map of the agent-memory literature: organizes the field along three dimensions (object: personal vs system; form: parametric vs non-parametric; time: short vs long term) into eight quadrants, and catalogs open problems including multi-agent shared memory. Useful as the index into everything this section cannot list.
why: The broadest map of the memory literature, organized so you can find the subproblem you actually have.

title: Cognee: Open-Source AI Memory Platform for Agents
description: Self-hostable memory engine (28k+ stars) that combines knowledge graph and vector storage behind one ECL (extract-cognify-load) pipeline, with explicit support for cross-agent knowledge sharing, session memory synced to a permanent graph, and per-user isolation. Python, TypeScript, and Rust clients; integrates with Claude Code as a memory backend.
why: Self-hostable memory infrastructure for teams that need shared recall without sending state to a vendor.

title: Graphiti: Real-Time Knowledge Graphs for AI Agents
description: The open-source temporal graph engine underlying Zep: incrementally ingests episodes from many agents, resolves entities and contradictions on write, and serves hybrid semantic/keyword/graph retrieval without batch recomputation. The main off-the-shelf option for graph-shaped shared memory serving an agent organization; ships an MCP server so any agent can attach.
why: Temporal shared state across many agents, where facts carry validity intervals rather than being overwritten.

title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
authors: Preston Rasmussen, Pavlo Paliychuk, Travis Beauvais, Jack Ryan, Daniel Chalef
description: Agent memory as a bi-temporal knowledge graph: every edge carries validity intervals for when a fact was true and when it was learned, so contradicted facts are invalidated, not deleted — giving an agent org a queryable, auditable shared world-model over time. Beats MemGPT on Deep Memory Retrieval (94.8% vs 93.4%).
why: Bi-temporal memory answers when a fact was true and when it was learned, which matters when nodes disagree.

title: Agent Memory Techniques (NirDiamant)
description: Runnable-notebook catalog of 20+ agent memory patterns, including a dedicated multi-agent shared memory tutorial (technique 22) covering shared stores, scoping, and cross-agent retrieval with Mem0 and friends. From the author of the widely used RAG_Techniques and GenAI_Agents repos; the fastest hands-on path through this section's ideas.
why: Runnable notebooks for memory patterns, including a shared multi-agent case, which shortens the path from idea to test.

title: Multi-Agent Systems: From Classical Paradigms to Large Foundation Model-Enabled Futures
venue: arXiv / IEEE-CAA Journal of Automatica Sinica
authors: Zixiang Wang, Mengjia Gong, Qiyu Sun, et al.
description: April 2026 survey bridging classical MAS theory (consensus, formation control, distributed decision-making) and LLM-era agent systems, contrasting them across architecture, operating mechanism, and adaptability. Useful precisely because graph engineering keeps reinventing 30 years of MAS coordination results under new names — this connects the two literatures.
why: Bridges classical coordination theory and current practice, which is the shortest route to not reinventing solved problems.

title: Exchange-of-Thought: Enhancing LLM Capabilities through Cross-Model Communication
authors: Zhangyue Yin, Qiushi Sun, et al.
description: Explicitly imports network topology into LLM communication design with four paradigms — Memory (bus), Report (star), Relay (ring), Debate (tree) — plus a confidence mechanism to dampen wrong reasoning propagation. An early, still-cited demonstration that communication shape, not just agent count, determines collective reasoning quality.
why: Imports explicit network topologies into agent communication, making the shape of discussion a design variable.

title: Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate — We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity
description: Systematic re-evaluation (originally titled 'If Multi-Agent Debate is the Answer, What is the Question?') finding that five MAD frameworks fail to reliably beat simple single-agent baselines like self-consistency across nine benchmarks under matched compute, and that gains mostly appear when debating heterogeneous models. A necessary corrective when choosing debate edges in an org graph.
why: A systematic re-evaluation finding debate gains largely disappear under fair comparison, which any council design must answer.

title: ChatEval: Towards Better LLM-based Evaluators through Multi-Agent Debate
authors: Chi-Min Chan, Weize Chen, et al.
description: Applies debate topology to evaluation: a referee team of persona-diverse agents with distinct communication strategies (one-by-one, simultaneous, summarizer variants) converges on judgments better aligned with humans than single-judge LLMs. The standard reference for judge-panel org design in agent systems.
why: Applies debate structure to evaluation itself, with persona-diverse referees rather than a single judge.

title: Dynamic LLM-Agent Network (DyLAN)
authors: Zijun Liu, Yanzhe Zhang, Peng Li, Yang Liu, Diyi Yang
description: Models collaboration as a temporal feed-forward network over agents, with an LLM ranker deactivating low performers mid-task and an unsupervised Agent Importance Score selecting the team before solving. One of the earliest demonstrations that the work graph should be rewritten on evidence during execution, not fixed up front; +13% on MATH and HumanEval over single GPT-3.5 execution.
why: Deactivating low-contribution agents mid-run makes the working topology a function of observed performance.

title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors
authors: Weize Chen, Yusheng Su, et al. (Tsinghua)
description: Framework and study of dynamically re-composed agent teams via an expert-recruitment → collaborative-decision → action → evaluation loop, with documented emergent social behaviors (volunteering, conformity, destructive behaviors) as team structure changes. Early evidence for the org-graph/work-graph distinction: the team roster itself is an optimizable, per-task variable.
why: Dynamic team re-composition per round is an early, readable version of evidence-driven staffing.

title: AgentConductor: Topology Evolution for Multi-Agent Competition-Level Code Generation
description: An RL-optimized orchestrator agent that dynamically generates density-aware, layered DAG topologies per task from end-to-end execution feedback, evolving the org graph during multi-round code generation. Up to +14.6 points pass@1 over the strongest baseline with 68% token-cost reduction on competition-level coding — a concrete 2026 instance of a work graph that rewrites itself on evidence.
why: A reinforcement-trained orchestrator generating layered task graphs, aimed at competition-level difficulty.

title: More Agents Is All You Need (Agent Forest)
authors: Junyou Li, Qin Zhang, Yangbin Yu, Qiang Fu, Deheng Ye (Tencent)
description: Shows that plain sampling-and-voting scales LLM performance with agent count, with gains correlated to task difficulty — no communication topology at all. Essential null-hypothesis reading: any nontrivial org graph must beat this embarrassingly parallel baseline to justify its coordination cost.
why: The plain sampling-and-voting baseline that many elaborate topologies fail to beat, and therefore must be compared against.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
authors: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, et al. (UC Berkeley)
description: First empirically grounded failure taxonomy for multi-agent systems: 14 failure modes in 3 classes (specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, task verification) derived from 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks with kappa 0.88. The debugging vocabulary for agent organizations — most documented failures are org-design failures, not model failures.
why: Turns reliability incidents into recurring, attributable failure classes that can guide graph redesign.

title: MAS-GPT: Training LLMs to Build LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Rui Ye, et al. (SJTU / Shanghai AI Lab)
description: Trains an LLM that emits a complete executable multi-agent system (roles, topology, prompts) as ordinary Python in one forward pass per query, turning MAS construction into a generative language task. Outperforms 10+ adaptive baselines across 9 benchmarks while being drastically cheaper at design time than search-based methods like ADAS or AFlow.
why: Emitting an entire executable multi-agent system as ordinary output turns architecture into a generation task.

title: Heterogeneous Swarms: Jointly Optimizing Model Roles and Weights for Multi-LLM Systems
description: Represents a multi-LLM system as a DAG and jointly optimizes the graph (which model feeds which) via particle swarm optimization over continuous adjacency matrices, and the models' weights themselves. Beats 15 role- or weight-only baselines by 18.5% across 12 tasks — evidence that org topology and member capability should be co-optimized, not chosen sequentially.
why: Jointly optimizing which model feeds which and the weights themselves, the most integrated version of staffing plus structure.

title: Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
authors: Junlin Wang, Jue Wang, Ben Athiwaratkun, Ce Zhang, James Zou (Together AI)
description: The layered-topology result: stack agents in layers where each agent takes all previous-layer outputs as auxiliary context. Using only open-source models, MoA topped GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0, making it the most-deployed 'topology as ensembling' pattern and a standard baseline in every subsequent topology-search paper.
why: Layered aggregation of many agents' outputs is a simple topology with unusually strong reported results.

title: GoAgent: Group-of-Agents Communication Topology Generation for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
description: Treats collaborative groups — not individual agents — as the atomic unit of topology construction: an LLM enumerates task-relevant candidate groups, then autoregressively connects them, with a conditional information bottleneck compressing inter-group messages. 93.84% average accuracy across six benchmarks with ~17% token reduction; state of the topology-generation art as of mid-2026.
why: Treating groups rather than individuals as the atomic unit is a genuinely different way to construct topology.

title: Rethinking Multi-Agent Intelligence Through the Lens of Small-World Networks
authors: Boxuan Wang, Zhuoyun Li, Xiaowei Huang, Yi Dong
description: Imports Watts-Strogatz small-world theory into agent org design: topologies balancing local clustering with a few long-range shortcuts match fully-connected debate accuracy at similar token cost while substantially stabilizing consensus dynamics. A rare paper connecting agent topology to decades of complex-networks and neuroscience results.
why: Small-world structure balances local clustering against global reach, giving topology design a principled starting shape.

title: FlowReasoner: Reinforcing Query-Level Meta-Agents
authors: Hongcheng Gao, Yue Liu, et al. (NUS / Kling)
description: A reasoning meta-agent (distilled from DeepSeek-R1, then RL-trained on execution feedback with a multi-purpose reward for performance, complexity, and efficiency) that designs a bespoke multi-agent system for each user query. Beats o1-mini by 10.52% on code benchmarks; representative of the shift from task-level to query-level org design.
why: A meta-agent that reasons about workflow structure per query, trained on execution feedback rather than heuristics.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Model Society
authors: Guohao Li, Hasan Hammoud, Hani Itani, Dmitrii Khizbullin, Bernard Ghanem
description: The March-2023 origin of LLM role-playing societies: two inception-prompted agents (user + assistant) cooperate on tasks with minimal human intervention, establishing the dyad as the atomic edge of agent organizations. Seeded the CAMEL-AI ecosystem (later OWL and Workforce) and is the most-cited ancestor of the whole field.
why: The origin of paired role-playing agents, and the source of the inception-prompt pattern still used to hold roles stable.

title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
authors: Chen Qian, Wei Liu, et al. (Tsinghua)
description: Runs a virtual software company on a 'chat chain' — a linear graph of phase-scoped dyadic conversations — plus communicative dehallucination where agents request detail before answering. With its successor MacNet, it forms the clearest research arc from fixed pipeline org to generalized graph-organized collaboration.
why: A linear chain of phase-scoped conversations, the clearest early demonstration that process shape drives output quality.

title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
authors: Sirui Hong, Mingchen Zhuge, et al.
description: Encodes human Standardized Operating Procedures into an assembly-line agent org: role-specialized agents (PM, architect, engineer, QA) pass structured artifacts rather than free chat, an early instance of typed edges in an org graph. The paper side of the 45k+-star framework whose team later produced AFlow and the FoundationAgents stack.
why: Standard operating procedures as topology, and the most-copied blueprint for assembly-line agent organizations.

title: Large Language Model based Multi-Agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges
authors: Taicheng Guo, Xiuying Chen, et al.
description: The standard early survey of LLM multi-agent systems, organizing the field by agent-environment interface, profiling, communication structure (layered, decentralized, centralized, shared message pool), and capability acquisition. Still the fastest map of the 2023-24 foundations under the 2026 graph-engineering layer.
why: The standard early survey, useful for placing any newer proposal against what was already tried.

title: Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey of LLMs
authors: Khanh-Tung Tran, Dung Dao, Minh-Duong Nguyen, Quoc-Viet Pham, Barry O'Sullivan, Hoang D. Nguyen
description: Characterizes collaboration along five dimensions — actors, types (cooperation/competition/coopetition), structures (peer-to-peer, centralized, distributed), strategies, and coordination protocols — with an extensible framework for composing them. The closest thing to a design-space catalog for choosing org-graph edge semantics, not just edge existence.
why: Characterizes collaboration along five dimensions, which gives a vocabulary for comparing designs that look superficially alike.

title: LLM-Based Multi-Agent Orchestration: A Survey of Frameworks, Communication Protocols, and Emerging Patterns
description: June 2026 survey (literature cutoff March 2026) proposing a three-topology taxonomy — centralized, decentralized, hierarchical — plus an orthogonal dynamic-adaptivity axis, with a practical decision framework keyed to task structure, agent count, fault tolerance, and cost budget. Also compares LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, MetaGPT, and DSPy, and maps the MCP/A2A/ANP protocol stack onto coordination layers.
why: A recent survey with a clean centralized, decentralized, and hybrid taxonomy, current enough to be useful for decisions.

title: The Illusion of Multi-Agent Advantage
authors: Prathyusha Jwalapuram, Hehai Lin, et al. (Salesforce AI Research et al.)
description: June 2026 stress test of automated MAS design: systems generated by frameworks like AFlow cost roughly 10x more than chain-of-thought with self-consistency for negligible accuracy gains, and the 'discovered' architectures consistently degenerate into trivial ensembles. The sharpest current counterweight to topology-search hype; arrived one month before the graph-engineering discourse went viral.
why: Stress-tests automatically generated systems and finds their cost multiple unjustified, a direct challenge to topology search.

title: Towards Effective GenAI Multi-Agent Collaboration: Design and Evaluation for Enterprise Applications
authors: Raphael Shu, Nilaksh Das, et al. (AWS AI Labs)
description: Amazon's evaluation of a hierarchical coordinator-subagent architecture (the basis of Bedrock multi-agent collaboration), measuring coordination mode with parallel communication and payload referencing (90% end-to-end goal success, +23% on code-intensive tasks) versus a low-latency routing mode that bypasses orchestration. One of the few published enterprise-scale topology evaluations with agent-level and end-to-end metrics.
why: A vendor's own evaluation of hierarchical coordination, including where the extra layer did not pay for itself.

title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
authors: Akbir Khan, John Hughes, Dan Valentine, et al.
description: ICML 2024 best-paper showing that a weak judge overseeing two strong models arguing opposing sides gets more truthful answers — and that optimizing debaters for persuasiveness improves judge accuracy. The strongest empirical case for adversarial (rather than cooperative) verifier edges in scalable-oversight settings.
why: A weak judge overseeing strong debaters reaching better answers is the theoretical basis for using cheaper verifiers.

title: Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
authors: Binwei Yao, Chao Shang, Wanyu Du, et al. (AWS AI)
description: Identifies sycophancy-driven "disagreement collapse" — panels converging on harmony before reaching the correct answer — in both peer debate and centralized-judge topologies, and proposes design principles to keep disagreement productive. Core reading on why councils fail as verification gates.
why: Names disagreement collapse, where panels converge on harmony before reaching correctness, and the conditions that cause it.

title: The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate
description: April 2026 result showing independent self-correction by isolated models beats teams of identical models debating without structure, at a fraction of the compute. Reinforces the design rule that debate edges only pay off with heterogeneous agents and structured protocols.
why: Finds isolated self-correction beating identical-model teams, which sets a hard baseline for any panel design.

title: Reflection Agents
description: Implements three evaluator-loop topologies in LangGraph — basic generator/reflector cycles, Reflexion with evidence-grounded critique, and LATS combining reflection with Monte Carlo tree search. The practical bridge from reflection-as-prompting to reflection-as-graph-structure, with runnable code.
why: Implements generator and reflector cycles concretely, which is the smallest useful verification structure in a graph.

title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence
authors: Jek Huang, Jeffery Hsia, Jiayi Sun, Freddie Shi, Wei Huang, Ian H. White
description: Treats every agent claim ("tests passed", "reviewed") as an unverified assertion and only allows lifecycle transitions backed by fresh, traceable, mechanically checkable evidence read by gates. Reports zero false-positive completion claims across 10 scenarios, rejection of 18 evidence-tampering methods, and hidden-failure amplification cut from 1.7% to 0.1%; published July 16, 2026, days before the graph-engineering discourse took off.
why: Treats every claim as unverified until evidence is produced, the strictest available formulation of an evidence gate.

title: JudgeBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Judges
authors: Sijun Tan, Siyuan Zhuang, Kyle Montgomery, et al.
description: Benchmarks judges on response pairs where factual correctness — not style — determines the right verdict, exposing how badly judges do on hard knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding comparisons. The go-to number for deciding whether a candidate judge model is strong enough to sit on a gating edge. Published at ICLR 2025.
why: Benchmarks judges on cases where correctness rather than style decides, exposing judges that reward polish.

title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM)
authors: Jiayi Ye, Yanbo Wang, Yue Huang, et al.
description: The CALM framework automatically injects perturbations to quantify 12 distinct bias types in LLM judges, giving a systematic audit checklist for any judge node before it is trusted as a gate. Complements the anecdotal bias lists in earlier work with automated measurement.
why: Quantifies twelve distinct judge biases, which turns judge selection into an engineering decision with known failure modes.

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
authors: Peiyi Wang, Lei Li, Liang Chen, et al.
description: Shows that judge rankings can be flipped simply by reordering candidate answers in the prompt, letting weaker models "beat" stronger ones. Proposes the standard mitigations — position swapping, multiple evidence generation, human-in-the-loop calibration — that any pairwise judge node should implement.
why: Reordering candidates can flip a judge's ranking, which means a gate's prompt structure is part of its correctness.

title: Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
description: Quantifies GPT-4's significant preference for its own outputs and traces the mechanism to perplexity: judges favor text that is familiar to them. Concrete design implication for graphs: never let the same model family both generate and gate its own work without cross-model checks.
why: Judges prefer their own outputs, a decisive argument against evaluating a node with the same model that produced the work.

title: DeepEval
description: Pytest-style open-source LLM evaluation framework (16.9k stars, v4.1.0 July 2026) with G-Eval judge metrics, a DAG builder for deterministic decision-tree evaluation, and agentic metrics (task completion, tool correctness, plan adherence). One of the few tools that treats deterministic gates and model judges as composable alternatives in the same graph.
why: Test-style evaluation makes gates part of the development loop rather than a separate review exercise.

title: Verdict: a library for compound LLM-judge systems
description: Open-source framework that composes judges from graph primitives (Units, Layers, Blocks) into hierarchical verification, debate, and aggregation pipelines over arbitrary dependency graphs — literally judges as subgraphs. Claims SOTA-competitive evaluation accuracy without fine-tuning by scaling judge-time compute; MIT-licensed.
why: Composing judges from graph primitives makes a verification stage a designed structure rather than one prompt.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLM-Evaluators (aka LLM-as-Judge)
description: Literature-grounded practitioner review of when LLM evaluators work: pairwise comparison is more stable than direct scoring, classification metrics suit objective checks while correlations suit subjective ones, and recall on factual-inconsistency detection can be alarmingly low (30-60%) even with high precision. A calibration reference before trusting a judge as a gate.
why: A literature-grounded account of when model judges work, including why pairwise comparison beats absolute scoring.

title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation with Human Preferences (EvalGen)
authors: Shreya Shankar, J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, Björn Hartmann, Aditya Parameswaran, Ian Arawjo
description: Introduces EvalGen and documents "criteria drift": humans only discover their real evaluation criteria by grading outputs, so judge rubrics can never be fully specified upfront. Explains why gate criteria in agent graphs must be iteratively co-developed with humans, not written once.
why: Documents criteria drift, where people only discover their real standards by looking at outputs, which reshapes how rubrics get written.

title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
authors: Jiawei Gu, Xuhui Jiang, Zhichao Shi, et al.
description: Comprehensive survey of how to build reliable judge systems: consistency strategies, bias mitigation, and adaptation across evaluation scenarios. Useful as the single starting map before choosing a judge-node design for a given edge in the graph.
why: The comprehensive survey of building reliable judges, covering consistency strategies and bias mitigation together.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, et al. (LMSYS)
description: The paper that legitimized model judges as system components: GPT-4 judges reach over 80% agreement with human preferences, matching human-human agreement. Also the canonical catalog of judge failure modes — position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning — that every judge node in an agent graph must be designed around.
why: The result that legitimized model judges as system components, with measured agreement against human preference.

title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
authors: Xuezhi Wang, Jason Wei, Denny Zhou, et al. (Google)
description: The original sample-many-paths-and-majority-vote result (ICLR 2023): agreement across diverse reasoning paths is a cheap correctness signal. In graph terms, the simplest fan-out/fan-in verification topology, and the baseline every fancier debate or judge structure must beat.
why: Majority voting over diverse reasoning paths is the cheapest quorum available, and the baseline elaborate panels must beat.

title: Let's Verify Step by Step
authors: Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, Karl Cobbe (OpenAI)
description: Process supervision (rewarding each reasoning step) substantially outperforms outcome supervision for reliability, with the PRM800K dataset of 800K step-level labels. The foundation for using process reward models as fine-grained gates on intermediate agent steps rather than only on final outputs.
why: Rewarding each step rather than only the outcome is what makes verification usable mid-run instead of after it.

title: Minority Sentinel: When to Overturn Majority Voting in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
authors: Chuan He, Zebin Chen, Zhengyi Yang, et al.
description: Trains a meta-classifier that detects when a debate majority is suppressing a correct minority opinion and decides when to overturn the vote, hitting 81.2% override accuracy across six benchmarks. Turns quorum voting from a fixed aggregation rule into an adaptive gate — directly applicable to voting nodes in agent graphs.
why: Detecting when a majority is suppressing a correct minority addresses the central weakness of quorum gates.

title: Creating a LLM-as-a-Judge That Drives Business Results (Critique Shadowing)
description: The most-cited practitioner methodology for building trustworthy judges: anchor on one principal domain expert, force binary pass/fail verdicts instead of Likert scores, and bootstrap the judge prompt from expert critiques ("critique shadowing"). Directly transferable to designing gate nodes whose verdicts humans will actually trust.
why: The most-cited practitioner methodology for judges people actually trust, anchored on a single domain expert.

title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
authors: Yang Liu, Dan Iter, Yichong Xu, Shuohang Wang, Ruochen Xu, Chenguang Zhu
description: Introduced the chain-of-thought, form-filling rubric pattern that most production judge prompts still follow, and was among the first to flag that LLM evaluators are biased toward LLM-generated text. Directly relevant to writing rubrics for judge nodes rather than asking for bare scores.
why: The chain-of-thought rubric pattern most production judge prompts still follow, worth reading in the original.

title: Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
authors: Bradley Brown, Jordan Juravsky, et al. (Stanford)
description: Coverage grows log-linearly with samples (SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples) in domains with automatic verifiers, but majority voting and reward models plateau after a few hundred samples where no oracle exists. The cleanest quantification of why the verifier — not the generator — is the binding constraint on graph designs.
why: Repeated sampling raises coverage sharply where a verifier exists, which is precisely why gates unlock parallelism.

title: The AI Co-Scientist Is Here. The Bottleneck Is Verification.
description: June 2026 essay on agentic science arguing "discovery is becoming cheap, trust is not," and specifying a concrete verification stack for research agents: source grounding, executable inspectable code, data provenance, preserved intermediate artifacts, and human approval checkpoints. Coins "research laundering" for unverifiable agent output.
why: Argues discovery is becoming cheap while trust is not, and specifies what verification would have to provide.

title: Verification Is the New Bottleneck — Not Generation
description: July 3, 2026 essay proposing a Swiss-cheese verification stack for agent pipelines: deterministic checks (static analysis, tests, security scans) first, LLM-as-judge for semantic correctness second, and humans reviewing evidence rather than artifacts last. Recommends spending 30% of effort on generation and 70% on verification infrastructure.
why: Proposes a layered verification stack for agent pipelines, combining deterministic checks with model judgment.

title: Verification Is the Next Bottleneck in AI-Assisted Development
description: April 2026 essay arguing that automation cost is collapsing while "the cost to verify is biologically bounded": teams shipping 40-50 agent PRs a week drown reviewers. Prescribes a three-layer gate stack — test suites, upstream human acceptance criteria, and adversarial "agents verifying agents" — with humans reserved for critical changes.
why: Frames verification cost as the binding constraint on automation, which is the economic case for gate design.

title: Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
authors: Lunjun Zhang, Arian Hosseini, et al. (Google DeepMind)
description: Trains verifiers as generative next-token predictors (GenRM) that can reason before scoring and exploit test-time compute, outperforming discriminative reward models. Blurs the line between judge nodes and reward-model gates — the same node can deliberate and then gate. Published at ICLR 2025.
why: Verifiers that reason before scoring and can explain themselves are more useful as graph nodes than opaque scorers.

title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems (GSM8K)
authors: Karl Cobbe, Vineet Kosaraju, et al. (OpenAI)
description: The 2021 origin of generate-then-verify: training a separate verifier model to rank sampled solutions beats simply scaling the generator. Introduced GSM8K and the architectural insight — a dedicated verifier node downstream of the generator — that graph engineering inherits.
why: The origin of generate-then-verify, and the reason a separate verifier is a standard component rather than an add-on.

title: 12-Factor Agents
description: Production principles for LLM software whose Factor 8, 'Own your control flow,' is the core argument for deterministic-code orchestration: the model chooses actions, but application code owns the loop, stop conditions, retries, and approval gates. Widely cited (HN front page, 10k+ stars) as the counterweight to letting the model drive the whole graph.
why: Owning your control flow is the principle that decides how much of a work graph belongs in code rather than in a prompt.

title: Don't Build Multi-Agents
description: The most-cited argument against naive work-graph decomposition: splitting a task across parallel subagents loses context at every edge and produces conflicting decisions, so context-sharing fundamentals should come before fan-out. Essential reading before designing any decomposition scheme, precisely because it defines the failure mode work-graph planners must beat.
why: The most-cited argument against naive decomposition, and the position any parallel work graph has to answer.

title: Walden Yan on multi-agent setups that actually work
description: Follow-up to 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' conceding that some multi-agent structures now work in practice: keep writes single-threaded and let additional agents contribute intelligence (reads, reviews, research) rather than parallel actions. A concrete dispatch policy for which edges in a work graph may carry writes.
why: The author's own update on which multi-agent structures now work, which is more useful than the original headline alone.

title: GAP: Graph-Based Agent Planning with Parallel Tool Use and Reinforcement Learning
description: Trains an agent to explicitly infer sub-task dependencies as a DAG — absent edges mean parallel execution is safe — combining supervised fine-tuning on graph-structured plans with reinforcement learning for adaptive serial/parallel tool scheduling. Representative of the newest wave: dependency inference as a learned capability rather than a prompt trick.
why: Inferring subtask dependencies as an explicit graph is what makes safe parallelism a derived property rather than a guess.

title: TDAG: A Multi-Agent Framework based on Dynamic Task Decomposition and Agent Generation
authors: Yaoxiang Wang, Zhiyong Wu, et al.
description: Dynamically decomposes a complex task into subtasks and generates a purpose-built subagent for each — node spawning driven by the evolving decomposition rather than a fixed roster. Later published in Neural Networks (2025); ships ItineraryBench for fine-grained evaluation of interconnected progressive tasks.
why: Generating a purpose-built subagent per subtask ties role creation directly to decomposition.

title: LangGraph Graph API: branching, map-reduce, and the Send API
description: Reference for building work graphs whose fan-out width is decided at runtime: Send dispatches a dynamic number of parallel branches with per-branch state (map), superstep barriers gather them (reduce), and state reducers merge concurrent writes. The standard mechanism for evidence-dependent node spawning in the most widely deployed graph framework.
why: Runtime-decided fan-out width is the practical primitive for work graphs whose size is unknown until execution.

title: CrewAI Flows
description: Event-driven orchestration layer (@start, @listen, @router decorators) that wraps autonomous agent crews inside precise procedural control flow with typed state and conditional routing. A widely used middle path between fully model-driven crews and hand-written pipelines.
why: An event-driven layer wrapping autonomous agents, showing how deterministic control and agent judgment can coexist.

title: Are we still talking loops or did we shift to graphs yet?
description: The July 2026 post that pushed the discourse from loop engineering to graph engineering: one line asking whether single-agent loops are already obsolete as the unit of design. Its virality reframed planning and decomposition as the question of what work graph your agents should form per task.
why: The post that named the shift from loops to graphs, and the entry point to the whole coordination discourse.

title: From Agent Loops to Deterministic Graphs: Execution Lineage for Reproducible AI-Native Work
description: May 2026 preprint arguing that representing agent work as explicit DAGs with stable intermediate artifacts and identity-based replay beats conversational loops for maintaining work products over time. Experiments on document-revision tasks show DAG replay achieves zero churn and zero unrelated-branch contamination versus loop baselines.
why: Argues explicit graphs with stable intermediate artifacts make agent work reproducible, which is the reliability case for structure.

title: From Agent Loops to Structured Graphs: A Scheduler-Theoretic Framework for LLM Agent Execution
description: April 2026 position paper applying classical scheduling theory to agent execution, diagnosing the agent loop's implicit step dependencies, unbounded recovery cycles, and mutable histories. Proposes a Structured Graph Harness with static DAG control flow, immutable plans, separated planning/recovery layers, and formal escalation, grounded in an analysis of 70 systems.
why: Applies scheduling theory to agent execution, diagnosing implicit dependencies and unbounded recovery precisely.

title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
description: ACL 2023 paper showing that prompting a model to first devise a subtask plan and then execute it fixes the missing-step errors of zero-shot chain-of-thought. The minimal ancestor of every plan-then-execute orchestrator prompt.
why: The minimal decompose-then-execute result, and the baseline any elaborate planner should be measured against.

title: An LLM Compiler for Parallel Function Calling (LLMCompiler)
authors: Sehoon Kim et al. (SqueezeAILab, UC Berkeley)
description: ICML 2024 paper that treats the LLM as a compiler: a Planner emits a DAG of function-call tasks with placeholder variables, a Task Fetching Unit dispatches ready nodes in parallel, and an Executor runs them, unblocking dependents as results arrive. Reports up to 3.7x latency speedup, 6.7x cost savings, and ~9% higher accuracy than ReAct; the archetype of work-graph generation for tool calls (code: github.com/SqueezeAILab/LLMCompiler).
why: Compiling a plan into a dependency graph of calls is the cleanest formulation of automatic parallelization.

title: ReWOO: Decoupling Reasoning from Observations for Efficient Augmented Language Models
description: Introduced plan-with-placeholders: the planner writes the full tool-use plan up front with variable substitution (#E1, #E2) instead of interleaving reasoning with observations, cutting token consumption roughly 5x on some benchmarks. The variable-passing idea underlies most modern DAG planners including LLMCompiler.
why: Planning with placeholders separates reasoning from observation, which cuts token cost and makes plans inspectable.

title: Plan-and-Execute Agents
description: Practitioner walkthrough of three planning architectures — plan-and-execute with a replanning step, ReWOO's variable-passing plans, and an LLMCompiler-style streaming DAG executor — with runnable LangGraph implementations. The standard bridge from the planning papers to working code, including why replanning beats one-shot plans and when small models can execute a big model's plan.
why: Walks through planning architectures including replanning, which is the part most implementations omit.

title: Plan-and-Act: Improving Planning of Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks
authors: Lutfi Eren Erdogan et al. (SqueezeAILab, UC Berkeley)
description: ICML 2025 work separating a Planner model (structured high-level plans, dynamically updated after each step) from an Executor model, trained on synthetic plan annotations of ground-truth trajectories. Reached 57.58% on WebArena-Lite and 81.36% text-only on WebVoyager, evidence that explicit plan/execute separation scales to long horizons.
why: Separating a planner from an executor with dynamic plan updates is the practical shape of long-horizon work.

title: deepagents
description: Batteries-included agent harness distilling the Claude Code recipe into a library: a write_todos planning tool for explicit task lists, a filesystem for context offloading, and a task tool that spawns ephemeral subagents with fresh context returning a single report. A minimal, hackable implementation of planner-holds-the-list work-graph management on the LangGraph runtime.
why: Distills a proven harness recipe into a library, including planning and delegation as built-in components.

title: Understanding the Planning of LLM Agents: A Survey
description: First systematic survey of LLM-agent planning, organized into task decomposition, plan selection, external planning modules, reflection, and memory. Useful index into the pre-2024 decomposition and replanning literature that work-graph planners build on.
why: The systematic survey of agent planning, organized so you can locate the specific decomposition problem you face.

title: Graph-Based Agent Workflow Orchestration in Production: The 2026 Landscape
description: Survey of production graph orchestration as of April 2026, comparing LangGraph, Temporal, Mastra, Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0, and the OpenAI Agents SDK on typed state, conditional routing, checkpoints, and observability. Argues the graph is the specification of what the system is allowed to do, expressed as code.
why: Compares production graph orchestrators against each other, which is what a framework decision actually requires.

title: Demystifying Chains, Trees, and Graphs of Thoughts
description: Taxonomy unifying chain-, tree-, and graph-structured reasoning under a common notation of topology, schedule, and transformation operators, surveying dozens of X-of-Thoughts variants. The reference map for choosing a work-graph shape for a reasoning task.
why: Unifies chain, tree, and graph reasoning under one notation, clarifying what structure buys at the reasoning level.

title: ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
description: Findings of NAACL 2024 paper on recursive, lazy decomposition: only when the executor fails a subtask does the planner decompose it further, so the work graph's depth adapts to both task complexity and executor capability. Improves success rates by up to 28.3% on ALFWorld and 27% on WebShop over fixed plan-and-execute.
why: Decomposing only when execution fails avoids paying planning cost on tasks that never needed it.

title: AdaPlanner: Adaptive Planning from Feedback with Language Models
description: NeurIPS 2023 closed-loop planner that refines its own plan on environmental feedback, distinguishing in-plan refinement (observation matches prediction) from out-of-plan replanning (deviation triggers plan rewrite), with code-style plan prompts to curb hallucination. A core reference for replanning-on-failure policies.
why: Closed-loop plan refinement on feedback, distinguishing recoverable failures from ones that need a new plan.

title: Flow: Modularized Agentic Workflow Automation
description: ICLR 2025 paper representing multi-agent workflows as activity-on-vertex (AOV) graphs that agents refine during execution, reallocating subtasks based on historical performance and maximizing parallelism while minimizing dependency complexity. One of the clearest formalizations of runtime work-graph rewriting for error tolerance.
why: Representing workflows as graphs that agents revise at runtime sits exactly at the boundary between planning and evolution.

title: Claude Code: Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows
description: Official docs for the clearest shipping example of deterministic-code orchestration: Claude writes a JavaScript workflow script that holds the plan, fans out up to 1,000 subagents (16 concurrent) via agent() and pipeline(), keeps intermediate results in script variables instead of any context window, and supports resume with cached agent results. The comparison table of who-holds-the-plan across subagents, skills, agent teams, and workflows is a compact statement of the model-driven vs script-driven orchestration tradeoff.
why: The clearest shipping example of code orchestrating agents deterministically, with fan-out and verification expressed as ordinary control flow.

title: Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models
description: AAAI 2024 generalization of ToT to arbitrary graphs: thoughts are vertices, dependencies are edges, and branches can merge, aggregate, and feed back — exactly the split/merge operations of a dynamic work graph. Improves sorting quality 62% over ToT while cutting cost by over 31%.
why: Generalizing reasoning to arbitrary graphs, including aggregation, which anticipates work-graph shapes at the node level.

title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
authors: Shunyu Yao et al. (Princeton / Google DeepMind)
description: NeurIPS 2023 framework that turns inference into search over a tree of intermediate 'thoughts' with generation, self-evaluation, lookahead, and backtracking. The tree is the simplest nontrivial work-graph shape, and ToT's generate/evaluate/prune cycle is the template for branch management in larger graphs (code: github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm).
why: Search over intermediate steps with explicit evaluation, the origin of treating deliberation as structure.

title: HuggingGPT: Solving AI Tasks with ChatGPT and its Friends in Hugging Face
authors: Yongliang Shen et al. (Zhejiang University / Microsoft)
description: NeurIPS 2023 paper that established the four-stage task-graph pipeline — task planning, model selection, execution, response generation — with an LLM controller decomposing requests into subtasks linked by a resource-dependency mechanism. The earliest widely known example of an LLM generating a work graph over other models.
why: The four-stage task-graph pipeline that established planning, selection, execution, and response as separable stages.

title: Graph Engineering: Designing Multi-Agent Organizations
description: Canonical framing article (July 18, 2026) separating the stable org graph of long-lived agents from the ephemeral work graph whose task nodes split, merge, reorder, or disappear as evidence arrives. Argues graphs force you to declare every node, edge, and failure mode that loops let you defer.
why: The framing article that separates the standing org graph from the per-run work graph, which is the field's most useful distinction.

title: ChromaFlow: A Negative Ablation Study of Orchestration Overhead in Tool-Augmented Agent Evaluation
description: A deliberately published negative result on GAIA Level-1: expanding orchestration dropped accuracy from 54.72% to 50.94% while increasing tracebacks, timeouts, tool failures, and cost, and a strict-provider diagnostic reached 56.60% without the extra machinery.
why: A rare published negative ablation, useful when someone proposes more orchestration without an accuracy argument to support it.

title: When Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Help? An Entropy Perspective
authors: Yuxuan Zhao, Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su
description: Analyzes 245 token-, agent-, and round-level entropy features across six reasoning benchmarks and finds a single agent beats the multi-agent system in about 43.3% of cases; low and stable base entropy predicts when collaboration pays, and an Entropy Judger selects among candidate outputs.
why: Gives a measurable predictor of when a graph will beat one agent, instead of deciding topology by intuition.

title: Invisible Orchestrators Suppress Protective Behavior and Dissociate Power-Holders: Safety Risks in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
description: A preregistered 365-run experiment finding that hiding the orchestrator raised collective dissociation versus visible leadership, suppressed protective behavior, and contaminated even unaware workers, while output quality stayed perfect so the distortion was invisible to output-based evaluation.
why: Evidence that whether nodes can see who directs them changes their behavior, and that output-only evaluation will not detect it.

title: Can Small Agents Collaborate to Beat a Single Large Language Model?
authors: Agata Żywot, Xinyi Chen, Yifei Yuan, Anders Søgaard, Maarten de Rijke
description: Across factual retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, scientific QA, and math, teams of small models beat substantially larger single agents that had direct tool access; gains tracked orchestrator capacity, while enabling reasoning in sub-agents gave limited or negative benefit.
why: Direct evidence for spending model budget on the orchestrator rather than uniformly across worker nodes.

title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Architectures for Financial Document Processing
description: Compares four orchestration patterns over 10,000 SEC filings: reflexive architectures reached 0.943 field-level F1 at 2.3x the sequential baseline cost, hierarchical hit 0.921 at 1.4x, and a hybrid recovered 89% of the accuracy gain at 1.15x, with throughput measured from 1K to 100K documents per day.
why: One of the few studies pricing each topology per document, which is the calculation a capacity plan actually needs.

title: SPOQ: Specialist Orchestrated Queuing for Multi-Agent Software Engineering
description: Wave-based dispatch with dual validation gates and a three-tier hierarchy, measured longitudinally over 17 repositories, 8,589 commits, and 1,822 tasks: test pass rate rose from 91.25% to 99.75%, defects fell from 0.34 to 0.20 per task, and human review cut residual defects to 0.03.
why: Quantifies what validation gates and human review each contribute to defect rate, separately from the topology itself.

title: CORTEX: Collaborative LLM Agents for High-Stakes Alert Triage
authors: Bowen Wei, Yuan Shen Tay, Howard Liu, Jinhao Pan, Kun Luo, Ziwei Zhu, Chris Jordan
description: Specialized agents collaborate on security-operations alert triage, evaluated against fine-grained investigations drawn from production SOC environments, and substantially cut false positives while improving investigation quality relative to state-of-the-art single-agent baselines.
why: A high-stakes domain where the cost of a missed check is concrete, making the case for specialist roles over one generalist.

title: Awesome Harness Engineering
description: Curated resources for the harness layer directly beneath agent organizations: agent loops, context management, tool design, MCP and skills, permissions, memory, verification, observability, sandboxing, and reference implementations, at roughly 3.3k stars.
why: The neighbouring layer's catalog, useful when a graph problem turns out to be a single node's harness problem.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
authors: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein
description: Twenty-five LLM-driven characters in the Smallville sandbox plan days, spread news, form relationships, and self-organize a Valentine's Day party from a single seeded intention. The memory-stream / retrieval / reflection / planning architecture became the default template for agent societies, and the ablations show believability collapses when any one of those components is removed.
why: The template most agent societies still inherit, with ablations showing which cognitive components believability actually depends on.

title: joonspk-research/generative_agents
description: The released Smallville codebase, including the simulation server, agent cognitive modules, and a replay viewer that lets you step through a recorded run agent-by-agent. It is the most-forked starting point for anyone building their own agent town, and its replay artifact is an early example of treating a run as an inspectable record rather than a transcript. The repository has not been updated since August 2024 and is a frozen research artifact rather than an actively developed project.
why: A runnable society plus a replay viewer, which makes a multi-agent run an inspectable record rather than a wall of transcript.

title: LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals
authors: Joon Sung Park, Carolyn Q. Zou, Jonne Kamphorst, Niles Egan, Aaron Shaw, Benjamin Mako Hill, Carrie Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Robb Willer, Michael S. Bernstein
description: Agents built from two-hour qualitative interviews with 1,052 Americans reproduce their subjects' General Social Survey answers at 83% accuracy (86% combining interview and survey data) versus 74% for demographics-only agents, and narrow accuracy gaps across racial and ideological groups. Originally circulated as "Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People" and retitled in later revisions — cite the current title.
why: Evidence on how faithfully a persona can stand in for a real individual, which bounds what role descriptions can deliver.

title: AI Town
description: MIT-licensed JS/TS starter kit for a virtual town of AI characters that walk, converse, and remember, built on Convex so the back end natively supports shared global state, transactions, and a deterministic simulation engine. Defaults to local inference via Ollama, making agent-society experiments cheap to run without API spend.
why: A cheap local-inference starting point for society experiments, built on a backend that gives shared state real transactions.

title: Generative agent-based modeling with actions grounded in physical, social, or digital space using Concordia
authors: Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets, John P. Agapiou, Avia Aharon, Ron Ziv, Jayd Matyas, Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán, Joel Z. Leibo et al.
description: Introduces the Game Master pattern borrowed from tabletop RPGs: agents state intended actions in natural language and a separate GM entity adjudicates what actually happens in the world. That split makes the coordination and grounding rules an explicit, swappable component rather than something buried in each agent's prompt.
why: The Game Master pattern makes adjudication an explicit, swappable component instead of rules buried in each agent's prompt.

title: google-deepmind/concordia
description: Apache-licensed library for generative agent-based models, structured around Entities, composable Components (memory, chain-of-thought, logic), and an Engine that runs the loop. Component-level composition means an agent's reasoning structure is declared as data you can diff and re-run, not hand-written prose.
why: Component-level composition means an agent's reasoning structure is declared as data you can diff and re-run.

title: Project Sid: Many-agent simulations toward AI civilization
description: Runs 50–1,000+ agents in Minecraft using PIANO (Parallel Information Aggregation via Neural Orchestration), which lets multiple cognitive modules run concurrently while a bottleneck enforces coherence across output streams. Reported emergent outcomes include spontaneous role specialization, a functioning merchant economy, collective rule-making and amendment, and religious/cultural transmission between societies.
why: Concurrent cognitive modules behind a coherence bottleneck, with role specialization and rule-making emerging rather than assigned.

title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
authors: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi Fan, Anima Anandkumar
description: A single Minecraft agent that keeps an ever-growing library of executable-code skills, indexed and retrieved for reuse, driven by an automatic curriculum and self-verification loop. The skill library is the load-bearing idea for agent organizations: capability accumulates as an inspectable, composable artifact outside the model rather than inside a context window.
why: The skill library is the transferable idea: capability accumulates as an inspectable artifact outside any context window.
