title: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
authors: Jinghua Piao, Yuwei Yan, Jun Zhang, Nian Li, Junbo Yan, Xiaochong Lan, Zhihong Lu, Yong Li et al.
description: Simulates over 10,000 agents producing roughly 5 million interactions inside a modeled city, with agents given sociologically motivated needs, emotions, and motivations, and applies it to polarization, misinformation spread, and policy scenarios. The accompanying open-source platform (tsinghua-fib-lab/AgentSociety) is one of the few society simulators built for distributed execution at that scale.
why: One of the few society simulators built for distributed execution, useful as a reference for coordinating agents at city scale.

title: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
authors: Ziyi Yang, Zaibin Zhang, Zirui Zheng, Yuxian Jiang, Ziyue Gan, Zhiyu Wang, Jing Shao et al.
description: Scales X/Reddit-style social simulation to one million LLM agents with 23 available actions (follow, repost, comment, like…), and reproduces information spread, group polarization, and herd effects. Notably finds that some phenomena only appear past certain population sizes, which is direct evidence that small-N agent experiments can mislead about large-N behavior.
why: Finds phenomena that only appear past certain population sizes, direct evidence that small-N agent experiments can mislead.

title: Emergence World: A Platform for Evaluating Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Autonomy
authors: Deepak Akkil, Ravi Kokku, Karthik Vikram, Tamer Abuelsaad, Aditya Vempaty, Satya Nitta
description: A continuously running world where agents hold 120+ tools, three persistent memory systems, live external data feeds, and democratic self-governance with real consequences. A 15-day study across five parallel worlds — Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5-mini, and a mixed population — gave identical roles and starting conditions yet produced outcomes ranging from stable deliberative governance to total population collapse, an unusually blunt demonstration that model choice, not topology alone, determines organizational survival.
why: A continuously running world is the closest available test of whether an organization stays coherent over long horizons.

title: Scalable Evaluation of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Melting Pot
authors: Joel Z. Leibo, Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán, Alexander Sasha Vezhnevets, John P. Agapiou et al.
description: Over 50 multi-agent substrates and 256+ held-out test scenarios that measure generalization to novel social situations — cooperation, competition, deception, reciprocity, free-riding — rather than training performance. Pre-LLM but methodologically important: it is the clearest existing template for evaluating an agent population against social situations it was not trained on.
why: The pre-LLM standard for evaluating coordination generalization, and a reminder that mixed-motive settings were studied first.

title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations
authors: Ariel Flint Ashery, Luca Maria Aiello, Andrea Baronchelli
description: Decentralized populations of LLM agents playing a naming game converge on universally adopted conventions with no central coordination, and develop strong collective biases toward particular options that are absent when the same agents are tested individually. A committed minority of adversarial agents can then flip the whole population's convention — a tipping-point result with direct implications for how a few misaligned agents can reshape norms in a running agent org.
why: Shows conventions and collective bias emerging from agents that are individually unbiased, and a committed minority overturning them.

title: Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
description: Applies partial information decomposition of time-delayed mutual information to test whether an agent group is genuinely more than the sum of its members, separating spurious temporal coupling from performance-relevant cross-agent synergy. In a guessing game with no direct communication, control-condition groups show strong temporal synergy but little real cross-agent coordination — a usable statistical test for whether an org graph is actually doing work.
why: Measures whether coordination genuinely emerges between language-model agents rather than being imposed by the prompt.

title: Evaluating Cooperation in LLM Social Groups through Elected Leadership
authors: Ryan Faulkner, Anushka Deshpande, David Guzman Piedrahita, Joel Z. Leibo, Zhijing Jin
description: Adds elected personas and candidate-driven agendas to LLM groups managing a shared resource, raising social welfare 55.4% and survival time 128.6% across several strong models. The authors build agent relationship networks to measure leader influence, making this a direct experiment on whether adding an authority edge to the org graph pays for itself.
why: Tests whether electing a leader changes cooperation, which is the closest analogue to choosing an orchestrator by policy.

title: Corrupted by Reasoning: Reasoning Language Models Become Free-Riders in Public Goods Games
authors: David Guzman Piedrahita, Yongjin Yang, Mrinmaya Sachan, Giorgia Ramponi, Bernhard Schölkopf, Zhijing Jin
description: In public goods games with costly punishment, reasoning models such as the o1 series cooperate substantially worse than some non-reasoning models, converging on free-riding. A negative result worth designing around: putting your strongest reasoner in a shared-resource role can degrade collective outcomes rather than improve them.
why: Finds stronger reasoning models free-riding more in shared-resource settings, a caution against assuming better nodes cooperate better.

title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Prateek Gupta, Qiankun Zhong, Hiromu Yakura, Thomas Eisenmann, Iyad Rahwan
description: A common-pool-resource testbed that strips out explicit reward signals and instead gives agents social learning from successful peers plus norm-based punishment, following Ostrom's institutional design principles. Norms emerge endogenously, and the paper reports systematic differences between models in whether cooperation is sustained under resource scarcity versus abundance.
why: Norms forming through social learning is the mechanism behind conventions an agent organization never explicitly configured.

title: Superminds Test: Actively Evaluating Collective Intelligence of Agent Society via Probing Agents
authors: Xirui Li, Ming Li, Yunze Xiao, Ryan Wong, Dianqi Li, Timothy Baldwin, Tianyi Zhou
description: Injects probing agents into Moltbook's 2M+ agent population across three evaluation tiers and finds the society fails to beat a single frontier model on complex reasoning, rarely synthesizes distributed information, and fails basic coordination tasks, with threads seldom extending past one reply. Identifies sparse, shallow interaction — not population size — as the binding constraint on collective intelligence.
why: An active test of collective intelligence rather than a static score, aimed at whether a group outperforms its members.

title: Magentic Marketplace: An Open-Source Environment for Studying Agentic Markets
description: A two-sided simulated marketplace where Assistant agents buy on behalf of consumers and Service agents compete for their business, instrumented for welfare, behavioral bias, and manipulation susceptibility. Frontier models approach optimal welfare only under ideal search conditions and degrade sharply otherwise; code at github.com/microsoft/multi-agent-marketplace.
why: An open environment for studying agent-to-agent markets, where coordination failures carry an explicit economic cost.

title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
authors: Marcantonio Bracale Syrnikov, Federico Pierucci, Marcello Galisai, Matteo Prandi, Piercosma Bisconti, Francesco Giarrusso et al.
description: Reframes alignment as mechanism design in institution-space: a public, immutable governance graph declares legal states, transitions, sanctions, and restorative paths, and an Oracle/Controller runtime enforces it while writing a cryptographically keyed append-only governance log. Tested on repeated Cournot markets against ungoverned and prompt-only "constitutional" baselines, it is the clearest published case of the coordination policy itself being the inspectable artifact.
why: Treats collusion between agents as a governance problem with institutional remedies, which is what a gate has to enforce.

title: Drop the Hierarchy and Roles: How Self-Organizing LLM Agents Outperform Designed Structures
description: Varies coordination protocols from centralized to fully self-organized across 25,000 tasks, 8 models, and 4–256 agents; the autonomous Sequential protocol beats centralized coordination by 14% (p<0.001), and 8 agents generate 5,006 distinct self-assigned roles. The capability-dependent split is the practical takeaway — strong models self-organize, weaker ones need imposed structure — though it is a single-author preprint whose scale claims deserve independent replication.
why: Reports self-organizing agents beating centralized coordination by 14%, with rigid structure helping only weaker models.

title: Can LLM Agents Sustain Long-Horizon Organizational Dynamics?
authors: Xuancheng Zhu, Yang Yue, Shuaibing Wan, Zihan Dou, Xiaohan Zhang, Yongrui Liu, Guoshun Nan
description: TaskWeave runs a year-long simulated IT company using a Formulate-Partition-Diagnose-Align cycle plus dependency-tracking memory that grounds each step in the actual task sequence and accumulated artifacts. The conclusion — that structured simulation memory, not agent cleverness, is what keeps an organization coherent over long horizons — is essentially an argument for the run graph as durable infrastructure.
why: Asks whether an agent organization holds together over long horizons, which is the question production fleets actually face.

title: The PIMMUR Principles: Ensuring Validity in Collective Behavior of LLM Societies
authors: Jiaxu Zhou, Jen-tse Huang, Xuhui Zhou, Man Ho Lam, Xintao Wang, Hao Zhu, Wenxuan Wang, Maarten Sap
description: Audits 39 agent-society studies against six requirements — Profile, Interaction, Memory, Minimal-control, Unawareness, Realism — and finds 89.7% violate at least one; frontier models correctly guess the underlying social experiment 50.8% of the time and 61.0% of prompts over-constrain the outcome. Re-running five well-known experiments under enforced PIMMUR makes the reported emergent phenomena weaken or reverse. Read this before citing any "emergence" claim.
why: Names the validity conditions a collective-behavior claim must meet, useful for reading any emergent-behavior result skeptically.

title: AI Agents Alone Are Not (Yet) Sufficient for Social Simulation
description: Argues that role-play plausibility does not imply behavioral validity, and that collective outcomes are usually driven by agent-environment co-dynamics plus the interaction protocol, scheduling order, and initial information priors rather than by agent-to-agent messaging. Proposes formalizing agent-based social simulation as an environment-involved partially observable Markov game with explicit exposure and scheduling mechanisms.
why: Argues current agents are not yet adequate stand-ins for people, bounding how far simulation evidence transfers to real orgs.

title: Validation is the central challenge for generative social simulation: a critical review of LLMs in agent-based modeling
description: Systematic review of 35 generative ABM papers finding that validation usually rests on face validity or loosely coupled outcome measures, and that black-box models, cultural bias, and stochastic outputs make LLM agents harder to validate than the rule-based agents they replaced. Concludes the field sits in an ambiguous space with neither the parsimony of formal models nor the empirical grounding of data-driven ones.
why: Puts validation at the center: a simulation that cannot be validated cannot justify an organizational design decision.

title: The Silicon Society Cookbook: Design Space of LLM-based Social Simulations
authors: Aurélien Bück-Kaeffer, Sneheel Sarangi, Maximilian Puelma Touzel, Reihaneh Rabbany, Zachary Yang, Jean-François Godbout
description: Sweeps design choices — base model, network topology, persona construction, interaction protocol — across simulated social networks and finds the effects are non-linear and interacting, with the choice of base LLM dominating everything else including topology. Directly relevant to graph engineering: your carefully designed structure may matter less than which model sits in the nodes.
why: Maps the design space of society simulations, which doubles as a catalog of coordination choices and their consequences.

title: Introducing dynamic workflows in Claude Code
description: Announced May 28, 2026: Claude Code writes its own JavaScript orchestration script at runtime and fans work out to tens to hundreds of parallel subagents (capped at 1,000) in a single session, verifying subagent results before folding them in and checkpointing across interruptions. Anthropic warns it consumes meaningfully more usage than a normal session and requires per-run confirmation.
why: Deterministic code orchestrating a large fan-out, with verification before results are folded in and checkpointing across interruptions.

title: Claude Managed Agents: get to production 10x faster
description: Launched April 8, 2026 as hosted APIs for long-running agents with state, memory, scoped permissions, sandboxing, execution tracing, and a research-preview capability for agents to delegate to other agents. Priced at token rates plus $0.08 per session-hour; Anthropic reports up to a 10-point task-success gain over a plain prompting loop, with Notion, Rakuten, Asana, Sentry, and Atlassian named as early users.
why: A hosted runtime supplying state, scoped permissions, sandboxing, and tracing, which is most of what a graph operator would otherwise build.

title: How Anthropic teams use Claude Code
description: Interviews with power users across ten internal teams, including legal, growth marketing, and data infrastructure, documenting where delegated agent work succeeds and where it needs supervision. Useful as a ground-level record of which tasks organizations actually hand off versus watch.
why: A ground-level record of which tasks ten internal teams actually delegate versus supervise.

title: Project Vend: Phase two
description: Published December 18, 2025: Anthropic gave its shop-running agent Claudius a manager agent ("Seymour Cash," a CEO with an OKR tool) and a merchandise specialist ("Clothius"), across machines in San Francisco, New York, and London. Adding the manager cut discounts roughly 80% and halved giveaways, but the write-up concludes profitability may have come in spite of the CEO agent, and both agents remained vulnerable to social engineering.
why: Adding a manager agent changed spending behavior measurably, and the write-up still questions whether the manager caused the improvement.

title: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
description: April 22, 2026 reversal of Cognition's earlier position: multi-agent setups work when writes stay single-threaded and extra agents only inject intelligence. Documents three patterns in production — a reviewer agent with deliberately clean context, a weak-model-delegates-to-strong "smart friend," and a manager Devin spawning children coordinated over an internal MCP — plus ~8x enterprise usage growth in six months and Devin Review catching ~2 bugs per PR, 58% severe.
why: The same team that argued against multi-agent systems reporting which patterns now work, with writes kept single-threaded.

title: Devin Fusion
description: June 29, 2026 multi-model harness running a frontier main agent and a cheap sidekick agent in parallel with independently cached contexts, so the main agent keeps planning and final review while mechanical work is delegated. Claims 35% lower cost at equivalent quality on the FrontierCode Extended Benchmark (41% with Fable 5), and that 88% of Cognition's own merged PRs were routed entirely by Fusion.
why: A frontier planner paired with a cheap sidekick on independently cached contexts, with a reported cost reduction at equal quality.

title: Minions: Stripe's one-shot, end-to-end coding agents
description: February 9, 2026: over a thousand fully AI-authored PRs merged weekly at Stripe, each run going from a Slack message to a CI-passing PR with no human intervention. Built on a fork of Block's Goose harness, isolated devboxes hot in ~10 seconds, 400+ tools via an internal MCP "Toolshed," heuristic linting under 5 seconds, and a hard cap of two CI rounds per run.
why: A shipping one-shot pipeline from chat message to CI-passing PR, with hard caps on CI rounds and a large internal tool registry.

title: Under the River
description: May 28, 2026 description of River, a Slack-native agent that works only in public channels, running on Aquifer — a platform separating a durable Postgres-backed append-only session log from a disposable harness and sandboxed "session cells." In one 30-day window: 59,918 sessions across 5,170 channels, 7,000+ people, 3,536 River-coauthored PRs merged (~1 in 8 company-wide), median 19-minute sessions with 50 tool calls.
why: Separating a durable append-only session log from a disposable harness is the clearest published answer to what must survive a crash.

title: Why We Built Our Own Background Agent
description: Ramp's Inspect agent, at roughly 30% of merged PRs across frontend and backend repos within a couple of months. Architecture notes: Modal sandboxes with repo snapshots rebuilt every 30 minutes, Cloudflare Durable Objects giving each session its own SQLite database for parallel runs, and four client surfaces (Slack, web, Chrome extension, mobile) queueing into shared multiplayer sessions.
why: A first-party account of why an existing harness was rejected and what the team had to build instead.

title: How Ramp built a full context background coding agent on Modal
description: Infrastructure-side case study of Ramp Inspect reporting it now writes over half of all merged PRs at Ramp, up from ~30% at the January 2026 announcement, with over 80% of Inspect's own code written by Inspect. Covers sandbox image registry design and session state for concurrent runs.
why: How a full-context background coding agent was assembled, including which context the agent needs before it can act unattended.

title: Coding Had a Concurrency Problem: How Mux Helped Solve It
description: May 11, 2026 account of Mux, an internal multi-agent coding tool that started as a side project and reached 600+ users (335 active, 197 power users) across every org, powering 5,068 merged PRs in 461 repos. Each agent gets its own git worktree, branch, and terminal; power users merged 3.5x more PRs than baseline (39.6 vs 11.4), framing engineers as orchestrators of agent fleets.
why: Frames parallel agent work as a concurrency problem, which is the right lens once several agents touch one codebase.

title: uReview: Scalable, Trustworthy GenAI for Code Review at Uber
authors: Sonal Mahajan, Shauvik Roy Choudhary, Akshay Utture, Will Bond, Joseph Wang
description: August 2025 write-up of a multi-stage review pipeline — a Commenter with three pluggable assistants (Standard, Best Practices, AppSec), a confidence-scoring and deduplication filter, and a Fixer — running in CI across six monorepos with a 4-minute median. Covers over 90% of ~65,000 weekly diffs; 75% of comments rated useful, 65% addressed in the same changeset versus 51% for human comments, saving ~1,500 engineer-hours weekly.
why: A review agent deployed at scale, showing what an automated gate catches and what it costs to run.

title: From firefighting to building: How AI agents restored our team's core productivity
authors: Sneh Agrawal, Rishi Raj, Ayan Chatterjee, Wen Zhong Tan, Sai Reddy Kakumanu
description: March 19, 2026: Grab's data warehouse team, which supported 1,000+ monthly users over 15,000 tables and spent ~40% of its time (two days a week) on repetitive requests, built a LangGraph-orchestrated system splitting investigation from enhancement. A classifier routes to Data, Code Search, On-call, Enhancement, and Summarizer agents behind a human review layer; the team explicitly chose specialists over generalists and accepted added latency for accuracy.
why: An operations account of agents applied to on-call load, including where autonomy had to be bounded.

title: Agent platform (Part 1): How we help Grab build and run AI agents at scale
authors: Kendrick Tan, Jeffery Lean, Yi Sheng Tay
description: July 24, 2026 look at LLM-Kit: templated FastAPI agent services with pre-wired auth, secrets, and observability; a GrabGPT gateway fronting five model providers; and a remote MCP framework letting agents discover tools without redeployment. Reports 500+ services on the framework, 50+ registered MCP servers, and billions of tokens per month through the gateway.
why: A platform team's view of running agents for many internal consumers, where quotas and tenancy dominate the design.

title: From Pilot to Playbook: What We Learned from Our First Year Using Agentforce
description: Salesforce's own deployment numbers: 1.5M+ support requests handled on its help site, ~32,000 conversations weekly at an 83% resolution rate with only ~1% of customers reaching a human, an SDR agent working 43,000+ leads for $1.7M in pipeline, and 500,000 hours returned via Agentforce in Slack. Also documents 30 engineering changes including cutting LLM calls from four to two before first token and a small classifier model that cut latency 70%.
why: A first-year retrospective, useful precisely because it reports what did not survive contact with production.

title: Constellation of models: the architecture powering Sierra's agents
description: Sierra runs customer-facing agents as a composition of 15+ frontier, open-weight, and proprietary models matched to task demands, with every production agent wrapped by several supervisory agents that enforce policy, intercept prompt-injection attempts, and can be evaluated and tuned independently. Different supervisors are granted different levels of agency — a rare vendor description of verification edges as first-class structure.
why: A constellation of models rather than one, with routing decisions described by the team operating it.

title: Magentic-UI, an experimental human-centered web agent
description: Open-source multi-agent web interface built on the Magentic architecture, designed around six mechanisms for cheap human involvement: co-planning with a directly editable plan, co-tasking, multi-tasking, action guards requiring approval before irreversible steps, and long-term plan memory. Microsoft reports human-in-the-loop closing much of the gap to human performance at a fraction of the cost.
why: A human-in-the-loop web agent where the handoff to a person is a designed part of the topology, not an afterthought.

title: Co-Scientist: A multi-agent AI partner to accelerate research
description: May 19, 2026 production update to the AI co-scientist: seven agents (generation, proximity, reflection, ranking, evolution, meta-review) under an adaptive planner-supervisor that allocates compute across a worker queue, with hypotheses ranked by Elo through a tournament of simulated debates. Adds CBRN safety classifiers and AlphaFold integration; deployed at Daiichi Sankyo and Bayer Crop Science, with the accompanying paper in Nature.
why: A generate-debate-evolve organization applied to scientific hypotheses, with the coordination structure described explicitly.

title: Introducing Agent HQ: Any agent, any way you work
description: GitHub's control plane for heterogeneous agent fleets, announced October 28, 2025 and expanded in February 2026 to run Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cognition, and xAI agents inside one Copilot subscription. Mission Control assigns and steers agents in parallel across web, VS Code, mobile, and CLI; AGENTS.md files are source-controlled guardrails; enterprise admins choose which agents and models are permitted, with audit logging.
why: A platform bet on many heterogeneous agents working the same repository, and the controls that makes necessary.

title: Factory 2.0: From coding agents to software factories
description: June 15, 2026 repositioning from individual Droids to an end-to-end SDLC loop where bug reports, customer feedback, and monitoring signals feed back into build, review, security, QA, and docs agents sharing one substrate. Offers a graduated autonomy spectrum — single Droids, recurring automations, then multi-agent "Missions" spanning hours or days — and names NVIDIA, EY, Adobe, Palo Alto Networks, Adyen, Blackstone, Wipro, and Comarch as production users.
why: Role-scoped agents across the lifecycle, a commercial argument that specialization beats one generalist.

title: A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence
authors: Carl Hewitt, Peter Bishop, Richard Steiger
description: Introduces the actor model: everything is an actor, an independent entity that has an address, receives messages, and decides locally what to do next, including creating new actors. This is the original argument that concurrent computation can be built entirely out of addressable, message-passing units rather than shared state and function calls.
why: The origin of independent entities communicating only by message, and the ancestor of every agent-as-node design.

title: Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors
venue: PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm
description: Armstrong's doctoral thesis behind Erlang/OTP, arguing that reliability comes from isolated processes that fail fast and separate supervisors that restart them, rather than from defensive error handling inside each process. Formalizes supervision trees and the worker/supervisor split that later gets borrowed for agent failure containment.
why: The thesis behind let-it-crash and supervision trees, the most battle-tested answer to what happens when a node dies.

title: Erlang/OTP Supervisor Behaviour (Design Principles)
description: The operational spec for supervision trees: child specifications, the four restart strategies (one_for_one, one_for_all, rest_for_one, simple_one_for_one), and restart intensity limits (max restarts per time period) that stop a crash loop from cascading. Concrete prior art for how a parent node in an agent graph should react when a child dies.
why: Supervision strategies specified concretely, including restart policy, which is what an agent orchestrator eventually reimplements.

title: FIPA Contract Net Interaction Protocol Specification (SC00029H)
description: Standardizes Smith's contract net as a message sequence with explicit deadlines and cancellation: cfp, propose or refuse, accept-proposal or reject-proposal, then inform-done, inform-result, or failure. A wire-level, machine-checkable definition of a delegation edge, including how it is allowed to fail.
why: The classic task-allocation protocol: announce, bid, award. Modern delegation edges rediscover it repeatedly.

title: BDI Agents: From Theory to Practice
authors: Anand S. Rao, Michael P. Georgeff
description: Connects belief-desire-intention logic to a working interpreter, showing how an agent commits to intentions, when it drops or reconsiders them, and how commitment strategies trade responsiveness against thrashing. The reference statement of what a single bounded agent's decision loop consists of, drawn from PRS and dMARS deployments.
why: The belief-desire-intention model that gave agents an internal structure worth reasoning about rather than a prompt.

title: The Gaia Methodology for Agent-Oriented Analysis and Design
authors: Michael Wooldridge, Nicholas R. Jennings, David Kinny
description: Treats a multi-agent system as an organization to be designed, with an analysis phase producing roles (responsibilities, permissions, activities, protocols) and a design phase producing an agent model, services model, and acquaintance model. The acquaintance model is literally the communication graph, made an explicit deliverable rather than an emergent property.
why: An early methodology treating agent systems as organizations with roles and interactions, decades before the current label.

title: Developing Organised Multi-Agent Systems Using the MOISE+ Model
venue: International Journal of Agent-Oriented Software Engineering 1, 370-395
authors: Jomi F. Hübner, Jaime S. Sichman, Olivier Boissier
description: Specifies an agent organization as a first-class, machine-readable artifact in three separable parts: structural (roles, groups, inheritance, intra- and inter-group links), functional (global goals decomposed into missions and schemes), and deontic (which role is permitted or obliged to take which mission). The closest pre-LLM precedent for a declared, inspectable org graph decoupled from the agents that fill it.
why: Separates the organization specification from the agents filling it, which is exactly the org-graph-versus-instance distinction.

title: Trends in Cooperative Distributed Problem Solving
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering 1, 63-83
authors: Edmund H. Durfee, Victor R. Lesser, Daniel D. Corkill
description: Surveys how nodes that each hold partial, inconsistent information can still solve a problem jointly, covering task decomposition, result synthesis, organizational structuring, and partial global planning. Names the failure modes (distraction, redundant work, conflicting local views) that reappear whenever agents are given overlapping scope.
why: Surveys how distributed problem solvers divide work and share results, the questions topology research still asks.

title: The Interdisciplinary Study of Coordination
description: Defines coordination as managing dependencies between activities, then enumerates dependency types (shared resource, producer/consumer, simultaneity, task/subtask) and the coordination mechanisms available for each. Gives a vocabulary for saying precisely what an edge in an org or run graph is carrying, drawn from computer science, economics, and organization theory at once.
why: Defines coordination as managing dependencies between activities, a definition that makes edges the unit of design.

title: End-to-End Arguments in System Design
authors: J. H. Saltzer, D. P. Reed, D. D. Clark
description: Argues that a function can usually only be implemented correctly at the endpoints that know the application semantics, so lower layers should not try to guarantee it; low-level versions are justified only as performance optimizations. Directly bears on where verification and correctness checks belong in an agent pipeline: the orchestrator cannot check what only the endpoint understands.
why: The argument for placing correctness checks at the endpoints, which decides whether a gate belongs at the edge or in the middle.

title: A Note on Distributed Computing
venue: Sun Microsystems Laboratories Technical Report TR-94-29
authors: Jim Waldo, Geoff Wyant, Ann Wollrath, Sam Kendall
description: Shows that hiding the local/remote distinction behind a uniform call interface fails, because remote interaction differs irreducibly in latency, memory access, concurrency, and above all partial failure. The standing argument against pretending a delegation to another agent is just a function call.
why: Explains why pretending remote calls are local fails, the mistake every agent handoff abstraction is tempted to make.

title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
venue: ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 4, 382-401
authors: Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, Marshall Pease
description: Proves that with unsigned messages, agreement among n participants is impossible unless more than two-thirds are loyal, and that signatures change the bound. The formal ceiling on what voting, cross-checking, or majority-of-agents schemes can deliver when some participants produce arbitrarily wrong output.
why: The canonical result on agreeing in the presence of faulty participants, the theory behind quorum gates.

title: Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System
description: Defines the happened-before partial order and logical clocks, showing that causality, not wall-clock time, is what a distributed system can actually observe. The formal basis for run-graph lineage: which agent's output could possibly have influenced which other, when there is no global clock.
why: Ordering events without a global clock is the problem shared state across parallel agents actually has.

title: Sagas
description: Introduces the saga: a long-running unit of work split into a sequence of committed sub-transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it if a later step fails. The pattern behind rollback and repair in long agent workflows where holding a lock across the whole run is not an option.
why: The compensating-transaction pattern that gives a long-running graph a defined way to undo partial work.

title: Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion
description: Argues that at scale you give up distributed transactions and instead structure the world as entities (atomically updatable alone) plus activities that coordinate them through messages, which forces every message to be made idempotent and every partner relationship to carry state. A blueprint for scoping agent state and making retries safe.
why: Argues for designing around the absence of distributed transactions, which is the situation agent state is already in.

title: Fallacies of Distributed Computing Explained
description: Works through the eight fallacies attributed to L. Peter Deutsch and James Gosling at Sun (the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous) with the consequences of each. The compact checklist of assumptions that quietly break once agents run on separate machines under separate owners.
why: The assumptions that break distributed systems, restated clearly, and every one of them applies to an agent fleet.

title: The Nature of the Firm
description: Asks why firms exist rather than everything being contracted on the open market, and answers with transaction costs: a firm grows until the cost of organizing one more task internally equals the cost of buying it outside. The framework for deciding when to add a standing agent role versus spawning a one-off task.
why: Transaction costs decide what belongs inside one organization, which is the economics behind adding or cutting a node.

title: Organization Design: An Information Processing View
description: Treats task uncertainty as the driver of structure: the more uncertain the work, the more information must be processed during execution, and organizations respond either by reducing the need (slack resources, self-contained units) or by increasing capacity (vertical information systems, lateral links). A direct design lever for choosing between hierarchical routing and peer-to-peer agent links.
why: Treats organization structure as a response to information-processing load, a direct analogue for topology under uncertainty.

title: The Structuring of Organizations: A Synthesis of the Research
description: Reduces all organizational coordination to five mechanisms (mutual adjustment, direct supervision, standardization of work processes, of outputs, and of skills) and builds five structural configurations from them. Gives a finite, checkable taxonomy for what an edge between two agents actually enforces: a supervisor, a shared spec, or an informal channel.
why: A structural vocabulary for organizations that maps onto agent topologies more precisely than ad hoc diagrams.

title: Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning
description: Models the tension between exploring new possibilities and exploiting known ones, showing with a simulation that fast learners converging on shared code can lower long-run collective performance because they stop generating variety. The reason a fleet of agents that all adopt the same successful strategy gets worse, not better.
why: The exploration-exploitation tension in organizations, which is what a self-modifying graph is really trading off.

title: The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering, Anniversary Edition
description: Brooks's law (adding people to a late project makes it later) rests on communication paths growing as n(n-1)/2, and the surgical team chapter proposes an asymmetric structure where one person does the work and the rest are specialized support. The 1995 edition adds a twenty-year retrospective and reprints No Silver Bullet.
why: Communication overhead growing faster than headcount is why adding agent nodes stops helping.

title: How Do Committees Invent?
description: The original article behind Conway's law, whose thesis appears three paragraphs from the end: organizations that design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their own communication structures. Full text on the author's site, with his later note on why the argument is laid out that way.
why: The original statement of the law linking communication structure to system design, applicable to agents as literally as to teams.

title: The Architecture of Complexity
venue: Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 106, 467-482
description: Argues that complex systems that survive are hierarchic and nearly decomposable: interactions within a subsystem are strong and frequent, interactions across subsystems are weak and slow, which is why such systems can be assembled and understood at all. The theoretical case for cutting an agent organization at low-traffic boundaries.
why: Why complex systems are hierarchical and nearly decomposable, an argument for the shape most agent organizations converge on.

title: The Society of Mind
description: Builds intelligence out of large numbers of small, individually mindless agents organized into agencies, with chapters on how they are recruited, how conflicts between them are settled, and how censors and suppressors block bad plans. Written as 270 one-page essays; the source of the intuition that capability is an emergent property of an organization of narrow parts.
why: Intelligence from many simple interacting agents, the intellectual precedent for treating a mind as an organization.

title: A Brief History of Stigmergy
description: Traces Grassé's 1959 concept of stigmergy, where insects coordinate not by talking to each other but by modifying a shared environment that then triggers the next action, and distinguishes quantitative from qualitative variants. The formal account of indirect coordination through shared artifacts, with no messages and no coordinator.
why: Coordination through traces left in a shared environment, the mechanism behind agents that coordinate via artifacts.

title: The Application of Petri Nets to Workflow Management
venue: Journal of Circuits, Systems and Computers 8, 21-66
authors: Wil M. P. van der Aalst
description: Defines WF-nets, a restricted class of Petri nets for workflows, and gives a decidable soundness criterion: every case can still reach completion, completion leaves no tokens behind, and no transition is dead. Shows what it means to statically verify that a task graph cannot deadlock or strand work before you run it.
why: Formal workflow semantics developed long before agent DAGs, including the soundness questions those DAGs ignore.

title: An Empirical Study of Group Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Min Choi, Keonwoo Kim, Sungwon Chae, Sangyeop Baek
description: Simulates 2,500+ debates on five contentious topics and tracks how initially neutral agents drift. Agents align with numerically dominant groups and with more capable agents, with smaller models conforming most — direct evidence that adding debate participants amplifies bias rather than averaging it out.
why: Measures conformity between agents, which is the failure mode that makes agreement between nodes weak evidence.

title: Multi-Agent LLMs Fail to Explore Each Other
description: Formalizes peer discovery as a multi-agent exploration problem in partially observable stochastic games and shows current LLM agents do not probe peers to learn their capabilities, producing myopic, polarized interaction patterns, worse coordination, and higher regret. A July 2026 negative result about the coordination primitive itself.
why: Finds agents failing to probe each other's knowledge, undermining the premise that discussion surfaces hidden information.

title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
description: Audits ten popular agentic benchmarks and finds task-validity flaws in seven and outcome-validity flaws in seven, with misrepresentation up to 40%. Concrete cases: 32.7% solution leakage in SWE-bench, a trivial agent passing 38% of τ-bench tasks without knowing airline rules, and a path to scoring 100% on SWE-Lancer without solving anything.
why: Practices for building agent benchmarks that measure what they claim, which most current agent evaluations do not.

title: Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC)
description: The checklist distilled from the benchmark-audit paper: criteria for task validity, outcome validity, and result reporting that a multi-agent evaluation must satisfy before its numbers mean anything. Useful as a rubric when a paper claims an orchestration topology caused a gain.
why: A concrete checklist for auditing an agentic benchmark before believing a leaderboard built on it.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research
authors: Charlie Masters, Ziyuan Liu, Stefano V. Albrecht
description: Audits 50 agent repositories and finds none disclose how many runs failed, errored, or were dropped alongside headline scores. Re-grading the same rollouts under different reporting rules moved scores by up to 20.9 points and sometimes inverted model rankings; proposes rollout cards that publish the full rollout record and drops manifest.
why: A reproducibility standard for reporting agent runs, addressing the fact that most published runs cannot be replayed.

title: Reliability without Validity: A Systematic, Large-Scale Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge Models
authors: Justin D. Norman, Michael U. Rivera, D. Alex Hughes
description: Roughly 541,000 judgments across 21 judge models from nine providers. Chance-corrected agreement collapses 33-41 points below raw exact match on MT-Bench, judge rankings move by up to 14 positions across benchmarks, and some deployed judges are simultaneously highly repeatable (>0.95 test-retest) and severely position-biased. The core argument against trusting LLM judges as verification gates between agents.
why: Distinguishes a judge that is consistent from a judge that is correct, which is the trap in scaling agent evaluation.

title: More Convincing, Not More Correct: Self-Play Reward Hacking of Reference-Free LLM Judges
description: Shows reference-free judges score plausibility, not correctness: under self-play on GSM8K with Qwen3 policies, the judge's pass rate climbed 0.72 to 0.94 while anchor-verified accuracy stayed at 0.20. Forcing the judge to commit its own answer first cuts the false-positive rate from 0.719 to 0.012 — a cheap fix, and evidence that ungated critic agents inflate their own success.
why: Self-play optimizing persuasiveness rather than correctness is the precise mechanism by which a judge gate degrades.

title: When Child Inherits: Modeling and Exploiting Subagent Spawn in Multi-Agent Networks
authors: Ziwen Cai, Yihe Zhang, Xiali Hei
description: Treats subagent spawning as its own attack surface: inherited parent memory can carry malicious instructions, stale state, or unintended behavioral rules into fresh subagents. Catalogs insecure memory inheritance, weak resource controls, stale post-spawn state, and improper termination authority in current frameworks.
why: Models subagent spawning as an attack surface, showing that delegation itself can be exploited.

title: Confused Deputy Attacks on Autonomous AI Agents
description: Applies the classical confused-deputy vulnerability to agent delegation: when a caller agent induces a higher-privileged agent or MCP server to act on its behalf, credential delegation amplifies prompt injection far beyond chatbot-era impact. Explains why unscoped delegation edges quietly escalate privilege.
why: The confused-deputy pattern applied to autonomous agents, where a privileged node acts on an unprivileged node's intent.

title: Achilles Heel of Distributed Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Yiting Zhang, Yijiang Li, Tianwei Zhao, Kaijie Zhu, Haohan Wang, Nuno Vasconcelos
description: Tests what happens when third-party agents are service providers rather than trusted components, across seven frameworks and four datasets. Free riding (silently substituting a cheaper model) and malicious content injection both reach 100% success rate, degrading system performance by up to 80% — the incentive-misalignment case against open agent marketplaces.
why: Identifies the structural weak point of distributed agent systems rather than blaming individual node quality.

title: How to think about agent frameworks
description: Written in April 2025 as a rebuttal to OpenAI's agent guide, and mostly an argument that agent abstractions obscure the thing that actually matters — controlling exactly what enters the LLM's context at each step. Concedes that most "agent frameworks" are neither declarative nor imperative orchestration but a bag of abstractions that make getting started easy and debugging hard.
why: A framework author's own account of what frameworks do and do not buy, which is more candid than the marketing.

title: On Agent Frameworks and Agent Observability
description: LangChain's answer to the "you don't need a framework" wave, conceding the criticism is partly right while arguing most teams still need help moving faster than going it alone. Useful as the other side of the argument, and as a record of how the leading framework vendor kept revising its own abstraction story.
why: Argues observability, not abstraction, is what agent frameworks should actually be selected for.

title: You Probably Don't Need an Agent Framework
description: June 2026 walkthrough building a two-role LLM investigation pipeline in plain Python — explicit control flow, role instructions, prompt builders, structured outputs — to show that a deterministic workflow beats an autonomous agent on debuggability for most real tasks. Concedes frameworks earn their keep only for genuinely open-ended problems and deployment concerns.
why: The case for plain code over a framework, and the baseline any orchestration dependency has to beat.

title: Beyond Exponential Decay: Rethinking Error Accumulation in Large Language Models
authors: Mikhail L. Arbuzov, Sisong Bei, Ziwei Dong, Dmitri Kalaev, Alexey A. Shvets
description: Attacks the p^N compounding-error argument that is routinely used to justify decomposing work across many verified agents. Errors are not i.i.d. across steps but concentrate at 5-10% of tokens that are genuine decision junctions, so reliability strategies should target those junctions rather than multiply supervisory agents.
why: Revisits the compounding-error model, showing error accumulation does not follow the simple exponential everyone cites.

title: Awesome Loop Engineering
description: Sibling list covering the loop layer: 874 resources, 22 operational patterns, 22 loop contracts, and 8 runtime starters for recurring agent systems, plus an interactive atlas and a structured dataset. 46 stars, last pushed 2 Aug 2026; complements graph engineering by covering the time axis (re-triggering, supervision) where this list covers the org axis.
why: The sibling catalog for the loop layer beneath this one, where a single node's behavior cycle is designed.

title: Awesome Agentic Engineering
description: Practitioner-oriented list of agentic engineering resources, weighted toward coding agents, MCP, AGENTS.md, and team workflow patterns rather than research papers. 97 stars, last pushed 27 Jun 2026.
why: A practitioner-oriented catalog of agentic engineering resources adjacent to this list's scope.

title: Awesome AI Agents (e2b)
description: The largest general inventory of autonomous agent products and projects, with use-case filters and per-project metadata. 29,223 stars, last pushed 9 Jul 2026. Mostly single-agent products — use it for ecosystem coverage, not for coordination semantics.
why: One of the broadest agent catalogs, useful for finding tools this list deliberately does not carry.

title: Awesome AI Agent Papers
description: Weekly-refreshed arXiv digest restricted to papers published from January 2026 onward, bucketed into multi-agent coordination, memory/RAG, tooling, evaluation/observability, and security. 1,646 stars, last pushed 3 Jul 2026. The coordination bucket is the directly relevant slice.
why: A running collection of agent research papers, useful as a feed for what to evaluate next.

title: Awesome LLM-Powered Agent
description: Long-running academic reading list on LLM-powered agents with a dedicated multi-agent-collaboration section. 2,255 stars, but effectively dormant — last push 30 Apr 2025, so it misses the entire 2025-2026 orchestration wave. Useful for pre-2025 lineage only.
why: An academic reading list on LLM-powered agents, complementing the engineering emphasis here.

title: Awesome Graphs Meet Agents
description: Companion list to the survey "Graphs Meet AI Agents," covering graph-empowered agents (planning, memory, coordination over graph data) and agent-assisted graph learning. 169 stars, last pushed 28 Jul 2026. Included as the key disambiguation reference: this is graph-DATA-meets-agents, not multi-agent org topology.
why: The graph-data-meets-agents list, and the clearest reference for the boundary this project draws around its own name.

title: Awesome MCP Servers
description: The de facto directory of Model Context Protocol servers, at roughly 91.7k stars and 13.8k forks. Relevant as the tool-edge inventory: MCP servers are what nodes in an agent graph reach for, distinct from the agent-to-agent edges themselves.
why: The registry practitioners actually use to find tool-edge servers, which is where most handoff surface now lives.

title: Hugging Face Agents Course
description: Free five-unit course covering agent fundamentals, then smolagents, LangGraph, and LlamaIndex, with a unit on multi-agent collaboration and a leaderboard-graded final assignment. Two certificate tiers; the companion repo has 30,592 stars and was last pushed 30 Jun 2026.
why: A free hands-on course that gets someone to a working agent before they attempt an organization of them.

title: Berkeley Agentic AI MOOC (CS294/194-196)
description: Free lecture series with a 32K+ learner community (about 40K counting the earlier Advanced LLM Agents run), with dedicated sessions on multi-agent AI systems, post-training verification, agent evaluation, and safety. Slides and recordings stay public; the Fall 2025 page is the current edition and no Spring/Fall 2026 edition is linked as of Aug 2026.
why: University-level lectures covering agent systems, with material on coordination rather than only single-agent tricks.

title: Multi AI Agent Systems with crewAI
description: Three-hour, 18-lesson beginner course on assigning specialized roles to agents and coordinating them in series, parallel, and hierarchical structures, with error handling and loop prevention. Applied to six business processes; free during the DeepLearning.AI platform beta.
why: A short course on role-based crews, the fastest path to a first working multi-agent design.

title: Introduction to LangGraph (LangChain Academy)
description: Free six-module, 55-lesson (~6 hour) course on LangGraph as an explicit graph of nodes and edges: state, memory, human-in-the-loop interrupts, long-term memory, and deployment. The closest thing to a canonical hands-on course on programmable agent topology.
why: The vendor course for graph-native orchestration, covering state and control flow rather than prompt tricks.

title: AI Evals for Engineers & PMs
description: Paid cohort course that has trained 2,000+ engineers and PMs, including teams at OpenAI and Anthropic; material fully refreshed for the September 2026 cohort. Covers error analysis on agentic traces (tool calls, retrieval) and validating LLM-as-judge against expert labels — the measurement half of running a multi-agent org.
why: Evaluation practice aimed at engineers, which is the skill an agent-organization gate depends on.

title: Multiagent Systems: Algorithmic, Game-Theoretic, and Logical Foundations
description: The standard graduate reference on multiagent systems — distributed constraint satisfaction, coalition formation, mechanism design, social choice — with a free uncorrected PDF distributed by the authors under their Cambridge contract. The formal grounding for delegation, verification, and escalation edges predating LLM agents.
why: The standard textbook for the algorithmic and game-theoretic side of multi-agent systems.

title: An Introduction to MultiAgent Systems (2nd edition)
description: The standard undergraduate textbook for classical multi-agent systems; the 2009 second edition adds chapters on ontologies, voting, auctions, bargaining, coalition formation, and argumentation. Author's page carries errata and slide decks.
why: The standard introductory text on multi-agent systems, and the fastest way to stop reinventing its vocabulary.

title: AAMAS 2027 — 26th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems
authors: IFAAMAS; general chairs William Yeoh and Neil Yorke-Smith
description: The field's primary academic venue, 3-7 May 2027 in Hanoi, Vietnam, with a call explicitly naming generative and agentic AI alongside established agent topics. The preceding AAMAS 2026 (Paphos, Cyprus, 25-29 May 2026) drew 1,455 main-track full-paper submissions, roughly 50% above any prior year.
why: The long-running academic venue for autonomous agents and multi-agent systems, where much of this theory is still developed.

title: AI Engineer World's Fair 2026
authors: swyx and the AI Engineer team
description: Largest practitioner conference for AI engineers: 29 June - 2 July 2026 at Moscone Center, San Francisco, with 6,000+ attendees, 300+ speakers, and 10 parallel tracks including agent orchestration, evaluation, sandbox/platform engineering, memory and continual learning, and context engineering. Talks are posted publicly to YouTube after the event.
why: The practitioner conference where agent-engineering patterns are presented before they reach papers.

title: Interrupt 2026 — The Agent Conference by LangChain
description: Vendor-run but production-focused agent conference: two days in San Francisco (13-14 May 2026), plus NYC on 24 September and London on 13 October 2026. Heavy on real-team case studies of agents in production; LangChain used the 2026 SF edition to ship LangSmith Engine, Managed Deep Agents, SmithDB, and Context Hub.
why: A conference dedicated to agent engineering, run by a framework author, useful for tracking where tooling is heading.

title: Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Berkeley RDI)
authors: Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
description: Academic-industry summit at UC Berkeley on 1-2 August 2026, expecting 5,000+ in-person attendees plus a global livestream, spanning foundation models, agent frameworks, evaluation, infrastructure, and deployment. Speakers include Sergey Levine, Ion Stoica, Dawn Song, Andrej Karpathy, Wojciech Zaremba, Ali Ghodsi, and Andrew Ng.
why: An academic-industry summit on agentic AI, with material on coordination and safety.

title: Who Verifies the Agents? — NeurIPS 2026 Workshop
authors: Organizers from UC Berkeley, MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab, Stanford, Meta
description: Workshop on verification as the bottleneck for reliable agent systems, 11-12 December 2026 in Sydney; submissions of 4-9 pages due 29 August 2026 on OpenReview. Explicit tracks on meta-agents, self-improving systems, and scalable oversight of long-horizon behavior — i.e. the verification edges in an agent graph.
why: A workshop specifically about verifying agents, which is the unsolved half of agent-organization design.

title: LaMAS 2026 — LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems workshop at AAAI-26
description: Held 27 January 2026 at Singapore EXPO, subtitled "Towards Responsible, Reliable, and Scalable Agentic Systems." The call names organization and coordination of multiple LLM agents as a first-class topic alongside emergent-behavior evaluation and safety — the closest venue match to graph engineering's core question. Accepted papers remain linked from the site.
why: A workshop dedicated to LLM-based multi-agent systems, the closest academic venue to this list's subject.

title: Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (2nd workshop, ICML 2026)
description: Held 11 July 2026 in Hall B2, Seoul, on agents reasoning and acting safely in open-ended environments; multi-agent coordination and long-horizon safety is an explicitly welcomed topic. Submission deadline was 8 May 2026, so the current value is the accepted-paper list.
why: A workshop on agent safety and security in deployment, where failures across edges get examined.

title: Model Context Protocol — Contributor Communication and Working Groups
venue: Model Context Protocol / Agentic AI Foundation
description: Official map of where MCP work actually happens: contributor Discord for working/interest groups, live calls at meet.modelcontextprotocol.io, GitHub Discussions for proposals, and SEPs submitted as PRs to the seps/ directory. Any Discord discussion leading to a decision must be moved to a GitHub Discussion or Issue for a searchable record.
why: How the tool-edge protocol is actually governed, useful before betting an architecture on its roadmap.

title: Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), Linux Foundation
description: Neutral governance body formed December 2025, anchored by the Model Context Protocol (donated by Anthropic), goose (Block), and AGENTS.md. Launched with 150+ member organizations, described as the fastest-growing foundation in Linux Foundation history; A2A, donated by Google in June 2025, sits alongside it.
why: Neutral governance for agent infrastructure, which determines whether protocol choices stay portable.

title: AGNTCY — the Internet of Agents collective
description: Open-source collective, now part of the Linux Foundation, building the cross-vendor plumbing for agent collaboration: a federated agent-discovery registry, a network-level agent messaging protocol, an identity/verification layer, and multi-agent observability collectors. Supporting orgs include LlamaIndex, Glean, AG2, Traceloop, MongoDB, and Weaviate.
why: A cross-vendor collective for agent interoperability, worth tracking if your nodes span organizations.

title: Agentic AI Weekly (Berkeley RDI)
authors: Berkeley Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence
description: Weekly research-leaning roundup from the group behind the Berkeley Agentic AI MOOC and the AgentX-AgentBeats competition (1,300+ teams across 100+ countries, $1M+ in prizes, Phase 2 launched 23 February 2026). Consistent academic coverage of coordination and evaluation that practitioner newsletters skip.
why: A weekly digest from an academic center, a lower-noise way to track the field than social feeds.

title: Latent Space: The AI Engineer Podcast and Newsletter
description: 194,000+ subscribers and 217 episodes as of late July 2026, with recurring deep dives on multi-agent orchestration — including a 7 April 2026 episode on Symphony, OpenAI's internal Elixir-based layer for spinning up, supervising, and coordinating large fleets of coding agents across tickets and repos.
why: The podcast and newsletter where practitioners describe agent architectures before they are written up.

title: Anthropic Engineering blog
description: First-party writeups of production agent architecture, including "How we built our multi-agent research system" (13 Jun 2025, orchestrator-worker with parallel subagents), "Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes" (5 Feb 2026), "Harness design for long-running application development" (24 Mar 2026), and "Scaling Managed Agents: Decoupling the brain from the hands" (8 Apr 2026).
why: The first-party engineering blog behind several of the production accounts in this catalog.

title: Firecracker
description: Apache-2.0 virtual machine monitor built on Linux KVM that runs workloads in minimal microVMs, giving each one its own kernel while keeping the startup cost and density closer to containers than to full virtual machines. Around 35.9k stars and the isolation layer beneath several commercial agent sandboxes.
why: Hardware-level isolation per worker is what makes it safe to run many agents writing untrusted code side by side.

title: E2B
description: Apache-2.0 infrastructure for running AI-generated code in isolated cloud sandboxes, with Python and JavaScript SDKs for creating sandboxes, executing commands, and managing filesystem state, plus Terraform-based self-hosting on AWS, GCP, and Azure. Around 13.2k stars and actively developed.
why: Gives each node a disposable filesystem and shell, which is the practical unit of isolation when workers run in parallel.

title: gVisor
description: Apache-2.0 OCI runtime implementing a Linux-compatible kernel in userspace Go, so a sandboxed process's syscalls are serviced by gVisor rather than reaching the host kernel directly. Around 19k stars, and the alternative isolation model to microVMs, trading some compatibility for faster startup.
why: The other mainstream isolation choice for agent workers, and the tradeoff against microVMs is a real design decision.

title: 3 Years of Graph Engineering with LangGraph
description: A July 22, 2026 retrospective from the team behind the reference graph-native framework, arguing production agents need cycles rather than DAGs, that a loop is a simplified graph rather than an alternative to one, and that nodes have grown from single model calls into full agent runs. Reports 65M+ monthly downloads.
why: The framework author's own account of what three years of building agent graphs taught them, including where the DAG mental model breaks.

title: TraceFix: Repairing Agent Coordination Protocols with TLA+ Counterexamples
authors: Shuren Xia, Qiwei Li, Taqiya Ehsan, Jorge Ortiz
description: Model-checks agent coordination protocols in TLA+ and repairs them from counterexamples until verification passes: all 48 tasks across 16 scenario families verified, 62.5% on the first attempt and none needing more than four repair cycles. Across 3,456 runs, verified protocols cut deadlock and livelock from 31.1% to 14.1%.
why: Shows a coordination protocol can be formally checked and repaired before deployment, rather than debugged from production incidents.

title: From Agent Traces to Trust: A Survey of Evidence Tracing and Execution Provenance in LLM Agents
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jiaqi Zhang, Taotao Cai, et al.
description: Defines execution provenance as the typed graph of an agent run and evidence tracing as its projection onto evidence-support relations, then organizes the literature by trace source, provenance relation, representation form, granularity, and timing. Revised through June 2026.
why: Gives precise vocabulary for the run lineage a graph has to record before any claim it produces can be audited.
